- Published
Environmental groups have criticised a pilot scheme that aims to make housing developers pay a new nature levy.
The government wants parts of Norfolk to be the first areas subject to its Environmental Delivery Plan (EDP).
In order to unlock space for thousands of homes, developers would pay money that could create new wetlands, fund deer culls and restore rivers.
But ecology experts fear that it would fail to tackle the sources of pollution, leaving vulnerable chalk streams still at risk.
Sally Haines, chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Ecology and Environmental Management, said: "While [actions outlined in the plan] would improve ecological habitats in the area, they won't necessarily address the pollution that will be going into the water.
"Unless you do that, you are not going to get good nature recovery."
The EDP, which would apply to much of central Norfolk and parts of The Broads, would pool cash from housebuilders.
It would be spent on measures to help offset pollution from new homes.
Norfolk's rare chalk streams, often described as England's rainforests, are particularly vulnerable.
Environment Secretary Angela Eagle calls it a "win-win" for development and nature, claiming it would unlock space for 15,780 homes that are currently stalled because of rules protecting rivers.
With developers paying Â£2,675 per house, it is hoped the levy will raise about Â£42m.
The scheme is designed to replace the more complicated nutrient neutrality rules that are in place, which were blamed for blocking the regeneration plan for the former Colman's Mustard Factory at Carrow Works in Norwich.
A government spokesperson said the introduction of a single levy would make life easier for developers.
Natural England is leading on the project and chief executive Marian Spain said: "Instead of tackling pollution piecemeal, site by site, we can now deliver conservation measures that make a real difference for rivers, wetlands and wildlife across Norfolk."
However, Haines said it was a "fallacy" to blame environmental concerns as the main stumbling block when building houses - pointing instead to a myriad of issues such as the availability of materials and labour, and land prices.
Under the proposals, restoration projects would be put together for the River Wensum, the Bure broads and marshes, and the River Yare catchment area.
One eye-catching policy is to put some of the cash towards deer management, including targeted culling.
Booming deer populations in The Broads are becoming a growing issue as the animals can cause damage to the environment through grazing.
People can submit their views as part of a consultation, external - which opened on 17 September and runs until 27 October - before Natural England submits its final plans to Eagle and her department.
Natural England hopes to roll out EDPs in other parts of England in the future.
The chief executive of Norfolk Wildlife Trust, Eliot Lyne, said his organisation needed more time to review the proposals.
But he said it was worried about wider changes to planning rules and how they affected natural habitats.
"We are concerned that it weakens existing protections for Norfolk's nationally and globally important wildlife sites such as chalk streams, wetlands and valley fens," he added.
Mark Dye, a chalk stream campaigner for the Gaywood River Revival group in west Norfolk, said: "Fundamentally, if you are polluting a chalk stream or a river and you're putting more and more pollution into that river, and not seeking to address the underlying causes of that, then it's only going to get worse."
Steve Turner, executive director of the Home Builders Federation, claimed pollution from farmers was a bigger issue than new homes and he criticised water companies for not investing in infrastructure to stop sewage entering rivers.

bf548c7f5a80.text:
- Published
Thousands of supporters of Pakistan's jailed ex-prime minister Imran Khan are marching to the capital Islamabad as they call for his release.
Concerns over the 73-year-old's health have grown louder in recent months. His family claims he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
The cricket star-turned-politician, who faces charges in more than 100 cases, was jailed for 17 years over corruption last year. Khan said all the cases against him are politically motivated.
Even behind bars, he remains a force in Pakistani politics, and demonstrations in support for him have led to deadly violence and crackdowns in the past.
Sunday's march, which began in Lakki Marwat, a city 275km away from Islamabad, had paused for the night and is expected to resume around midday local time on Monday.
Originally scheduled for last week, it was postponed to allow for talks between the government and Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party but the talks ended in a deadlock.
Khan, who faces charges ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, was first imprisoned in August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year.
Sohail Afridi, chief minister for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province ruled by PTI, expects that the march will make its way to a town about 80km (50 miles) west of Islamabad by Thursday.
"[By then] this movement will have reached every corner of the country and every square will have become a centre of activity," he said on Sunday, urging the people to "play an active role in the political process".
Authorities in Islamabad have stacked up shipping containers to block key access routes to the capital city.
The PTI said talks with government failed because authorities rejected the party's request for access to Khan so that its leaders could consult him on national and political issues.
The party also said it had demanded that Khan be given an immediate medical examination and treatment.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi meanwhile accused Afridi of "sabotaging" negotiations, saying the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government had backed out of earlier commitments on counter-terrorism issues, according to Pakistan's local media reports.
In August, Khan was briefly transferred from jail to a state-run hospital for medical examination and treatment following complaints about his deteriorating health. The doctors later deemed him "medically fit".
The intervention was the most significant relief Khan has received from the courts since he was imprisoned in 2023 on corruption charges, which he says were politically motivated.
Khan's family and the PTI, however, criticised the authorities for defying a court order that he be examined by physicians at a specific private hospital.
On 20 September, Khan's sister Aleema Khanum was arrested in the eastern city of Lahore.
The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as the country's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.
His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.
At least eight people died in the protests and the army had to be called in to quell the violence.
Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urging Khan be accorded proper medical care.

Millions of Brazilians took to the polls on Sunday for the first round of the country's presidential elections.

Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday.
Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Ãdouard Geffray said.
He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests.
Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.
High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
On Friday, French Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests.
The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons".
"There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Ãdouard Geffray claimed.
"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before".
On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez.
Over 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according the AFP news agency, with around 85% of them minors.
Organisers of the protests have called for the demonstrations to continue on Tuesday after accusing the government of a lack of "concrete measures", according to AFP.
On Sunday, French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said his government is taking further steps to "address the difficulties faced by high school students and educational staff".
He said this includes ensuring classes continue, improving facilities, better organising school days and making the French university admissions platform more transparent.
Lecornu also said the government is accelerating the review of its "vandal-pays" bill to ensure that people responsible for damage bear the cost of their actions.

Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator.
On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island.
"We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter.
"Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues."
The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning.
On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft.
The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).
Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard.
"This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening.
"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."
Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.
Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News.
FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).
Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net.
"You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"
The pilot's response was inaudible.
"You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe.
The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.
An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue".
The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".
Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations.
"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

US President Donald Trump says he has created a new taskforce focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.
The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday.
It comes after the president signed an executive order on 29 September to rename AI as Super Intelligence, after previously saying the word artificial made it sound "fake".
Trump also said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" pact.
"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote.
Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research, Engineering Emil Michael and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will also be part of the taskforce.
It will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
The taskforce's chief, Clayton, took office as the US national intelligence director in August after Trump's original choice, Bill Pulte, was rejected by lawmakers.
On AI, Clayton has previously said: "When something's both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."
Clayton previously served as US attorney for the Southern District of New York, overseeing several prominent cases, including the drug trafficking case against former Venezuelan President Nicholas Maduro.
The announcement of the taskforce follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.
In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public.
"The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this âtechnology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.
Trump has dismissed calls for stronger oversight and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves.
The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google.
On the same day, the president signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
Some experts have questioned the logic of the rebranding, arguing that the use of "super intelligence" could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems.
Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm's AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI.
"SpaceX is a super intelligence company", Musk wrote.
The Tesla boss has recently been brought back into the US government to be part of a project to study the future of war.
Musk previously served in the Trump administration, heading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, before his tenure ended in a public spat with Trump.

"I was hurting inside, so I came to tell my story."
These were Seo Mi-hyeon's first words to the police.
Seo, who has an intellectual disability, struggles to form long sentences and can only communicate through brief words and gestures. But her memories of the abuse inflicted upon her were clear.
She was one of three residents at a state-run care home in South Korea who were sexually assaulted by the home's director, in a case that has shocked the country and raised serious questions about state care for the disabled.
Earlier this month, a court in Seoul sentenced the director - who has only been identified by his surname Kim - to 15 years in prison. Kim is appealing the conviction.
The court had heard that some residents were made to call the director "Dad", which prosecutors said illustrated the unequal relationship between Kim and those in his care.
The ruling came nearly two years after Seo, who is in her 40s, first disclosed the abuse to her mother.
We have changed Seo's name and the names of another victim in this story to protect their identities.
'I just endured it'
Seo first began living in Saekdongwon, a care home for the intellectually disabled, in 2016.
The institute, located in the city of Incheon, is fully subsidised by the state and still houses some 33 residents, although it has been asked to close down in light of this case.
According to Seo, the abuse began shortly after she began living there, with Kim visiting her at night or in the early hours of the morning to rape her.
Speaking through her lawyer Ko Eun-young, Seo said there was no adult at the facility she could speak to about the abuse, adding that she felt that other staff members would not help her. The care home has not responded to this allegation.
That was her life for almost 10 years, until the case came to light in February 2025, when Seo suffered a head injury.
She said it happened one of the times Kim tried to sexually assault her. She had blocked him with her hands, causing him to throw a glass at her.
Her lawyer told the court that the care home took Seo to hospital and informed her mother about the incident only after the wound on her head had been stitched up.
According to Seo's lawyer, Seo's mother had asked to see CCTV footage to establish how her daughter had been injured, but the facility refused, saying they were not authorised to release it.
As a result, her mother brought her home and decided to withdraw her from the facility. It was only after Seo was told that she would not have to return to the home that she disclosed the sexual abuse to her mum, who then reported it to the police.
"I thought it was safe to speak because I was told I didn't have to go back to Saekdongwon," Seo told the BBC via her lawyer.
When asked how she had managed on her own for so many years, she said: "I just endured it."
A police investigation into Seo's account was then widened to other residents.
They found at least two other alleged victims, including Lee Mi-Na, who said that she was also raped by Kim.
Earlier this month, a judge found all three victims' testimony credible.
He was sentenced to 15 years in jail for raping Lee and Seo, five years less than the original sentence prosecutors were asking for. He has denied all allegations and has since appealed the ruling.
For the third victim, Kim was found guilty of a lesser charge of sexual violence, with the judge saying the charge of rape against her was dropped as they could not find conclusive evidence that "force or threats [were used] that rendered the victim unable to resist".
A joint response committee made up of disability rights and other civic groups have criticsed this ruling, saying a victim's ability to resist an assault should not impact the verdict they receive.
The committee has also criticised the investigation process, saying there was a failure to identify more potential victims.
In November last year, following the initial allegations of abuse, local authorities from Ganghwa County had commissioned a team from Woosuk University to conduct an in-depth assessment of Saekdongwon's residents.
The report, which was submitted to the court as evidence, found indications that many more residents - at least 10 - could have been sexually assaulted by Kim.
But during the trial, the court did not address this finding.
According to local media reports, police had struggled to establish details of alleged abuse when interviewing residents, because most of them had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating. Some residents reportedly gave answers unrelated to the questions or did not respond at all.
Kim has not responded to allegations that he may have abused more residents.
Jeon Ji-su, the professor who led the Woosuk research team, told the BBC that investigators had accepted "only the accounts of people who could describe the abuse in complete sentences".
But activists said that this reliance on verbal testimony meant the police failed to recognise residents with greater communication difficulties as victims.
"If victims express their experiences differently from the way we expect, shouldn't the state make a greater effort to hear their voices?" said Baek In-seong, of Hansahoe, a counselling centre for survivors of sexual violence with disabilities.
Police have said that "while there may have been shortcomings in individual instances, these should not be taken as representative of the investigation as a whole".
Rights groups have also criticised others who have sought leniency for Kim.
Ahead of the verdict, a total of 13 petitions seeking leniency were said to have been submitted to the court. One of them, from a social welfare organisation, asked the court to take into account the defendant's "contribution to the welfare sector".
Welfare advocacy group Gyeol condemned the petitioning organisations, saying: "Past service in the welfare sector does not exempt anyone from accountability."

718b9217c0eb.text: President Trump's economic data keeps getting stronger. His economic polling keeps getting worse by the day. Why it matters: The midterms are less than a month away, and the administration is circling the drain on voters' No. 1 issue. It may be too late to change that, but it's also not clear anyone has much of a plan to try. What they're saying: "If I say 'oh, people are wrong, the economy is great,' then it looks like I'm insensitive. And if I then go into why the economy is great, then it looks like I'm insensitive," National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett said Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union." "It's true that the polls, which have gotten the president's success wrong every time, have been saying that people are looking a little bit depressed about the economy. But if you look at their actions, the actions speak way louder than words," Hassett added, citing spending and default data. The big picture: There is ample evidence the economy is, statistically speaking, relatively strong. 💰 Economic growth is solid and accelerating. 💪 The labor market is relatively stable . 💵 The K-shaped economy is ending as lower-end wages rise. 🛍️ Public and private data say consumers are spending more than ever. Yes, but: People feel lousy. ☹️ The Conference Board's consumer confidence index is at a 12-year low. 🐘 Republican sentiment in particular is eroding at its fastest rate since the Great Financial Crisis, per University of Michigan data. 🪫 38% of voters told the latest CBS News poll their personal finances are fairly or very bad — a reflection, perhaps, of the fact that inflation has outpaced wage growth for months now. (When respondents were asked what they think about when they rate the economy, 91% said "prices.") 👎 73% disapprove of President Trump's handling of the economy, per the latest AP-NORC survey, the lowest rating he — or President Biden — ever had. (69% say Trump's handling of cost-of-living issues has been worse than they expected in his second term.) Friction point: When voters go to the polls, they don't bring the latest release from the Bureau of Economic Analysis with them. They bring their feelings, and those are very bad. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told " The Axios Show " the administration wasn't going to repeat the Biden-era mistake of telling people how to feel. But Trump himself said last week that Republicans weren't doing a good enough job of messaging . The intrigue: So far, Trump's strategy seems to be the rich-uncle theory, which doesn't appear to be paying off with voters. He continues to promise $5,000 checks for every adult citizen if Republicans win the midterms — a $1.3 trillion bombshell that most people don't believe he'll ever pay. On Saturday, he promised seniors $2 billion in Medicare rebates , a big number that works out to about two weeks' worth of premium payments. Between the lines: Some of the tension comes from the nature of the economic boom, an AI-fueled bonanza that nonetheless appears to be leaving many ordinary Americans behind. It's not a K-shaped economy, says Krishna Guha, head of economics at Evercore ISI, but a "gator economy" — as in an alligator's mouth, where the bottom stays flat and the top is pointing to the sky poised to chomp. The bottom line: There's good reason to think the economy's not that bad. There's even better reason to think voters don't care. Emily Peck contributed reporting.

The number of young Americans who say theyâre âthrivingâ is near a low point while the share of middle-age adults who say the same is at a nadir, underscoring the level of relative dissatisfaction among these key demographic groups ahead of the midterms.
Only 44% of adults ages 18 to 29 describe themselves as thriving, according to Gallup, 20 points lower than the high measured in 2010. Forty-five percent of adults 30 to 44 say the same; both figures have declined in the years since the COVID-19 pandemic.

c31d3a0e07ea.text: Latino voters, whose dramatic shift toward President Trump helped power his 2024 victory, are moving sharply back toward Democrats ahead of the midterms, two new national polls show. Why it matters: Republicans built pieces of their 2026 strategy, including newly drawn House districts in Texas and Florida, around the assumption that Trump's historic Latino gains would endure. A reversal is complicating that bet in key races. Trump's breakthrough with Latino men was among the clearest signs of a changing GOP coalition in 2024. Two years later, those gains look far less durable, though Democrats haven't recovered all the ground they lost in the last decade. The latest: A new NBC News/Telemundo poll found Latino voters preferred Democratic control of Congress 59%–35% — a 24-point advantage, double the margin the same poll found in 2024. A new CBS News/YouGov poll tells the same story: Hispanic likely voters favor Democratic House candidates 60%–39%. Zoom in: Latino men have undergone a particularly strong political whiplash. Hillary Clinton won Latino men by 31 points in 2016, according to the Edison National Election Pool exit poll , and Biden won them by 23 points in 2020. But in 2024, Trump won them by 10 points. NBC now finds Latino men preferring Democratic congressional control 53%–39%. Stunning stat: About one in seven Latino voters who say they backed Trump in 2024 now want Democrats to take control of Congress. A majority of Latino voters say their congressional vote will be a signal against Trump. Driving the shift: The economic squeeze felt by Latino voters hasn't changed much, but who they're blaming has. Nearly two-thirds of Latino voters say their income is falling behind the cost of living in the NBC poll, almost exactly where that number stood in 2024. But 78% disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living. Democrats now hold a 21-point advantage on handling the economy, after Trump held a 4-point edge over Harris in NBC's 2024 poll. Trump's mass-deportation agenda has also sparked backlash: 67% say Trump's enforcement has gone too far. The enforcement campaign has also become personal: 31% say they or someone close now carries ID because of ICE concerns, and 27% know someone detained or deported. Yes, but: Polling voters a month before a midterm isn't the same as measuring who actually turns out. Pew found that Trump's 2024 Hispanic gains were driven largely by changes in who voted that year, not by Biden voters switching to Trump. In the NBC poll, 17% of voters said they or someone close to them was considering not voting in person because of fear of immigration enforcement. Between the lines: Despite all this, Democrats haven't repaired their brand with Latino voters. Their net favorability has actually fallen by one point from 2024, but the GOP's has fallen by 18 points. In 2016, 55% of Latino voters viewed the Democratic Party positively and 24% negatively — a 31-point net positive rating. Today, it's 41% positive and 42% negative. Republicans have still made lasting inroads: Just 16% of Latino voters viewed the GOP positively in 2016, compared with 27% today. But negative views have also risen, from 57% then to 62% now. What we're watching: Both parties are fighting over a large and growing Latino electorate in key races across Arizona, California, Florida and Texas.

f625378bd03a.text: The iPhone Duo isn't even out yet but developers are already having fun with the new design, creating apps that turn Apple's first foldable smartphone into everything from an accordion to a retro Walkman. Why it matters: Clever apps that couldn't exist on a traditional iPhone could help persuade early adopters to fork over nearly $2,000 for Apple's first foldable. Flashback: It's reminiscent of the early days of the iPhone, when developers turned its giant touchscreen and sensors into virtual versions of familiar objects, such as the virtual lighter apps whose flame flickered and swayed as the phone moved. Zoom in: Among the apps is Duo Man , a music player that turns the latest iPhone into a portable cassette player reminiscent of Sony's Walkman. Users open the Duo to choose an album and "insert" a cassette, then close it to start listening. Even the clicks and static are actual recordings from a real Walkman. It's the brainchild of indie app developer Vidit Bhargava, who created it during a four-hour hackathon last week. "I love the Walkman," he said. "I was just staring at it. I was like, this thing opens exactly like the iPhone Duo. What if your iPhone Duo was your Walkman, and you had to open up the door to change the album, and once you closed it, it would start playing the music." Bhargava has a particular affinity for the Walkman, having previously altered one of the vintage players to only work when a person is moving. Zoom out: Developers are finding ways to make the fold itself part of the software. The four-hour San Francisco hackathon where Duo-Man was born produced 73 submitted Duo projects, ranging from games to music tools and a virtual pop-up book. Accorduon turns the hinge into the bellows of a virtual accordion: The faster you fold and unfold the phone, the louder the instrument plays. Crate , which took first place at the same hackathon where Duo-Man finished second, turns the Duo into a beat machine, with folding controlling effects and snapping the phone open triggering a musical drop. Foldtales uses the hinge to create a virtual pop-up book, with castles, trees and other objects rising as the phone opens. Twofold uses the partially folded screen to hide each player's pieces in virtual versions of classic tabletop games. And Delta developer Riley Testut is working on Duo support that could make the foldable iPhone resemble another familiar hinged gadget: Nintendo's dual-screen DS. My thought bubble: Apple is years behind Samsung and Google in releasing a foldable phone. But its large developer ecosystem could help it catch-up quick. And the timing could turn out to be fortuitous. Developers are getting a new piece of hardware just as AI coding tools are making it faster and easier to turn a quirky idea into working software. What we're watching: Whether the initial burst of experimentation produces enduring apps — and whether Apple sells enough Duos to reward developers for building custom apps.

Medications can snowball as we age. Pill organizers pile up. Prescriptions that are no longer necessary can mix with other drugs to create concerning side effects.
“Once you get to six or seven prescription medications, you get a nearly 100% chance of some sort of side effect or intolerance,” said physician K. Eric De Jonge, director of geriatrics at MedStar Washington Hospital Center.
Paula Span writes “The New Old Age” column for The New York Times and KFF Health News. She joined WAMU’s Health Hub on Sept. 30 to talk about common medications — from aspirin to benzodiazepines — that some older patients are overusing.
Span shared tips for keeping loved ones safe and said it’s important for patients and caregivers to be proactive.
“Doctors prescribe medicine based on the evidence available at the time. But science doesn’t stop,” Span said. “Your doctor might not be up on the latest research. And patients get into a routine. They may not question if they still need the drugs they’ve been taking.”
Experts and pharmacists say: Check with your doctor to make sure the meds you’re taking are still right for you.

New York City is running out of places to dump its trash.
In the latest draft of the city’s once-a-decade solid waste management plan, the sanitation department warns that the landfills receiving much of the city’s garbage are filling up fast.
More than two-thirds of the city’s municipal waste is transported to landfills hundreds of miles away. Yet, under current permits, the state is projected to run out of landfill capacity for that garbage within 16 to 25 years.
As communities upstate push back against new and expanding landfills, the city may have to send its trash farther away. While efforts to divert more waste from landfills have made progress, experts say the city remains heavily reliant on landfill and waste incineration.
The state’s largest landfill, Seneca Meadows in the Finger Lakes region, has applied for an expansion permit, but nearby communities have opposed the effort.
As landfills expand, they generate more methane, a greenhouse gas 86 times more potent than carbon dioxide in the near term. The Seneca Meadows landfill is the single largest source of methane emissions in New York state.
Another environmental concern is leachate, a mixture of rainwater and toxins from landfill trash. Though it’s supposed to be pumped out and treated, some older landfills leak into the soil beneath and eventually into groundwater, spreading toxins to local waterways.
Landfills also emit small amounts of hydrogen sulfide and ammonia, gases that can cause unpleasant odors and immediate health effects, such as coughing and eye irritation.
“Who wants to have the landfill near them expand?” asked Craig Benson, an environmental engineer who has spent much of his career studying landfills. “But everybody wants their trash taken away.”
“Nobody Wants it to Grow”
Seneca Meadows towers over the warehouse and offices where Mark Pitifer works for Waterloo Container, a company that sells glass packaging to wine manufacturers across the Finger Lakes and beyond. Pitifer said that he smells the landfill at least once a week on his way to work.
“You get out of your car, you get hit with a raw, rotten stench,” he said. “Sometimes it’s more of a gassy smell. Today, it was a raw garbage smell.”
Trash from New York City accounted for around 20 percent of the waste trucked to the landfill in 2024. Queens alone sent 221,000 tons of solid waste there.
The Town of Seneca, where the Seneca Meadows landfill is located, passed a law in 2016 that required the landfill to close when its permit expires in 2025. After Seneca Meadows Inc., the landfill operator, sued to challenge the law, the New York State Appellate Court ultimately declared it invalid. The company has since applied to expand the landfill.
While the state’s Department of Environmental Conservation weighs the request, the landfill can continue operating—as long as it doesn’t exceed its current capacity.
By the end of 2024, the landfill had just eight months of permitted capacity remaining, according to the most recent report filed with state regulators.
But that estimate is not fixed. Benson, a professor emeritus at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, and dean of engineering emeritus at University of Virginia, said landfill operators can often extend a site’s permitted capacity by further compressing waste as it decomposes. A landfill’s remaining life can vary depending on how it is managed and how much waste it accepts in a given year.
Documents that Seneca Meadows Inc. submitted to state regulators show the company wants to increase the landfill’s height by about 70 feet, making it more than 840 feet high—almost as tall as Rockefeller Center in New York City. The expansion would extend the landfill’s life by 15 years, the company estimates.
“It’s a horrendous idea,” said Yvonne Taylor, the vice president of Seneca Lake Guardian, an environmental nonprofit that opposes the landfill expansion. “Nobody wants it to grow except for people who work at the landfill.”
While EPA records show that the landfill emits benzene, a known carcinogen, a June investigation that Seneca Lake Guardian advocated for did not find a direct link between the landfill and elevated cancer rates.
The organization sued the landfill in 2024 to stop its expansion, claiming that the odors it emits are a nuisance and violate locals’ rights to breathe clean air, as set out in the state’s Green Amendment. A judge dismissed parts of both parties’ complaints and stayed the case while Seneca Lake Guardian and Seneca Meadows Inc., the landfill company, appeal the decision.
Seneca Meadows Inc. did not respond to requests for comment.

Benson said local opposition is often the primary obstacle to building or expanding landfills. Expansion is often the better choice, especially if the management company has an unproblematic history, he said.
The Ontario County Sanitary Landfill, which in 2019 accepted 144,000 tons of municipal solid waste from Queens, received just 2,100 tons of construction debris from the city in 2024, according to reports filed with the state Department of Environmental Conservation.
In 2024, the town board voted to close the landfill when its permit expires in 2028. An analysis commissioned by county leaders found that the closure would require the area to ship its waste to other landfills, increasing costs through long-haul transportation.
The potential closure of Seneca Meadows could be a significant problem not just for the state, but for the entire region.
“If this capacity is lost at Seneca Meadows, these tons will be diverted to remaining landfills and [waste-to-energy] facilities, potentially with a dramatic tightening of the available disposal capacity in the region,” the analysis commissioned by Ontario County determined.

Democrats on the Senate Banking Committee are renewing their calls for Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte to appear before Congress after he sidelined its internal watchdog earlier this month.

They also highlighted Pulteâs other moves, like appointing himself as chair of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac; laying off employees; accusing Trumpâs political enemies of mortgage fraud; and serving simultaneously as acting director of national intelligence.
The letter provides a useful road map for how Democrats would scrutinize the agency if they win a majority of either chamber this fall. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, the Nevada Democrat who led the effort, pushed for passage of a bill last week that would require the FHFA internal watchdog receive whatever funding it requested.
Scott and FHFA did not return requests for comment.

The News
The winner of Senate control would snatch one of the biggest tangible prizes of the midterms: control over President Donald Trumpâs nominees.
If Democrats are in charge, donât expect many of Trumpâs picks to move at all.
âIf the nominees are as crappy as his present ones, very few of them are going to get through. If he sends us a new [Defense Secretary Pete] Hegseth, I bet he wouldnât pass the Senate,â Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told Semafor in a pre-election interview. âItâs the quality of the candidate that matters. Thus far, Trump has a record of notoriously bad candidates.â
Democrats are favored to take the House, which would limit big bipartisan breakthroughs on legislation next year. But if Republicans can hold the Senate, theyâd at least retain the ability to confirm Trump nominees â most notably, lifetime judicial appointments.
Schumerâs comments confirm that Democratic control of the Senate under Trump would turn the battle to confirm Senate nominees into trench warfare, with committee chairmen able to bottle up Trumpâs picks easily and Schumer able to simply not put them on the floor.
Perhaps a handful of judges would be confirmed, but Cabinet secretaries would face long slogs. Thereâs also little hope that a Democratic majority would confirm a Supreme Court nominee â should a vacancy arise â after then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnellâs blockade of Merrick Garland during the Obama years.
âA Democrat-controlled Senate will without any question block every single one of President Trumpâs nominees. This includes every cabinet member and every judge who is committed to upholding the Constitution,â said Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo. â[Schumer is] not going to change his playbook of obstruction and opposition.â
Know More
Itâs been more than a decade since the presidentâs party lost control of the Senate during a midterm election. After the 2014 red wave, Senate Republicans gave former President Barack Obama few lower-level judges, blocked a Supreme Court seat from being filled, and even blocked his attorney general nominee, Loretta Lynch, from confirmation until the Senate passed a human trafficking bill.
Thereâs no way around a judicial nominee blockade, but Trump can lean on acting officials in the executive branch. If Republicans do lose Senate control, look for the GOP to use its blunt confirmation tools â including confirming large tranches of nominees â in November and December to accomplish as much as they can before Schumer takes control again.
There are currently 27 judicial vacancies at the district level and 10 nominees to fill those, mostly in Republican states. There are also a handful of nominees ready to be confirmed to federal appeals courts.
If Republicans hold the chamber, they will probably prioritize judicial appointments for the next two years.

For many Okinawa locals, the arrest of a US soldier accused of robbing and killing a woman in a hotel room has reignited decades of frustration over crimes involving US military personnel there.
"Honestly my first reaction was, 'Not again,'" 52-year-old longtime Okinawa resident Ai Sato told the BBC.
"Nothing has changed since I was a child. How many times are we going to repeat the same thing, create more victims, cause their families to suffer, and ultimately, cause the people of Okinawa to grieve?"
Akemi Oshiro, a 62-year-old Ginowan resident shared similar sentiments.
"I know we shouldn't get used to terrible things like this, but because they keep happening, I've stopped being surprised," she told the BBC.
Okinawa hosts the largest US military presence in Japan. It is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops.
US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday. Police say an investigation is underway and that Ballard is in Japanese custody because the alleged crime was unrelated to official military duties.
Whether a US service member is acting in the performance of official duty, external or not can determine which country has primary jurisdiction. When Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect is under US custody, they can retain custody until Japan brings charges.
Ballard was assigned to III Marine Expeditionary Force and stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City.
The Okinawa prefectural police say 39-year-old Anna Yagi was found dead early 3 October in a hotel room in Naha.
Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings. Local media citing police have reported that Yagi appeared to have been strangled with a cord.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi registered an official protest with Washington. But residents like Sato feel that's far from enough.
"I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades -- that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously."
"I want Prime Minister Takaichi to call President Trump directly, someone with whom she has been emphasizing as having a close relationship with, and discuss concrete measures to prevent this from happening yet again," she said.
Following news of the suspected murder, people in Japan have been voicing anger with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice with one user saying: "Enough is enough."
Over the past few years, a number of accidents and crimes have led to growing local opposition to the US presence on the island.
The 2016 rape and murder of a 20-year-old local woman saw tens of thousands of protesters demonstrate against the heavy US presence there. A former US marine subsequently received a life sentence for the crime.
The US currently has about 55,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, with the heaviest concentration based on the tropical island prefecture. Okinawa is one of the country's smallest prefectures by size, but 70% of the land used exclusively by the US military in Japan is located there.
In 1972, Okinawa prefecture was returned to Japanese control after United States forces occupied the islands at the end of the Second World War. Since then, there have been 6,409 arrests for criminal offenses related to US military personnel, according to Okinawa Prefectural Government.
Locals say the significant US presence has stirred resentment over a number of issues from crimes including rapes, assaults, and drunk-driving accidents to local disturbances such as noise and aircraft crashes.
In 1995, three US servicemen abducted, beat, and raped a 12-year-old schoolgirl as she walked home from a stationery store.
In 2025, a US Marine was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a Japanese woman.
"Even 80 yeas after the war, Okinawa where we live is a place that is so unnerving," 48-year-old mother of two boys Hitomi Miyagi told the BBC.
"We will not stop raising our voices hoping for an Okinawa, where we can live in peace."

Chalk it up to Canadiansâ go-along-to-get-along instincts, but the race to shift the cost of the AI buildout â $7 trillion over the next decade, by Brookfieldâs estimate â from the hyperscalers themselves to external money managers is making strange bedfellows.
Brookfield has a joint venture with Nvidia to buy up to $100 billion of AI infrastructure assets. Itâs also in a consortium arranged by the chipmaker to corral another $500 billion alongside Apollo, Blackstone, and KKR â some of Brookfieldâs fiercest rivals.
Data centers, as well as the hardware inside them and the power plants feeding them, are basically the same as bridges, ports, and other unsexy but economically fundamental stuff that firms like Brookfield exist to build, own, and operate â albeit âon a much larger scale and happening much faster,â he said. There will still be plenty of losers among data-center financiers, he said. For power projects, heâs wary of gas, which is slow to deploy, and keener on fuel cells, onshore renewables, batteries, and nuclear.

Which offers the best returns?
Down-the-fairway, mature renewables â onshore wind and solar, battery storage â are absolutely seeing the most growth and have the most market participants. Initially itâs done by independent capital providers who look to build and hold the assets. Once the asset class grows, you begin to see banks syndicate the financing. Other capital participants come in, whether itâs private credit or insurance. That is exactly whatâs happened within AI infrastructure. The only thing thatâs different about this one is itâs happening on a much larger scale and happening much faster.
Iâve never seen competitors at the same table this often. How do you think about places where you want a deal to yourself versus sharing it â and sharing the returns â with your competitors?
Weâre seeing one of the biggest energy buildouts in history. Weâre seeing global trade rewired with an increasing focus on resiliency and production of critical goods closer to home. These are mega-trends that require far more capital than what has traditionally been available from both governments and even the public markets. So why can you get five or six of the leading players at one table? Because thereâs enough to go around for all of us.
But if everyone is in this trade, whatâs going to differentiate winners and losers?
While itâs easy to paint everything with a single wide brush, there is going to be a dispersion of who performs well and who has some disappointing results. To be absolutely clear, weâre not doing every opportunity we see. We are doing the tiniest fraction. And even with that very tight filter, we can deploy a tremendous amount of capital.

Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, read a Google summary or make an online bank payment, a data centre is working behind the scenes.
Now Scotland is part of a global race to build many more of them - on a massive scale.
The explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) over the past few years has seen tech firms scrambling to build new "hyperscale" data centres, including some which would rank among the biggest in the world.
Plans are in place to build at least 23 giant AI-powered data centres.
Supporters say they are vital for the future and could bring billions of pounds in investment, as well as thousands of jobs.
Opponents fear the impact of their size on local communities, the vast amounts of energy they use and even the noise they will make.
So what exactly are data centres, and why have they become one of Scotland's most controversial planning battles?
What is a data centre?
From the outside, data centres look like a factory or a warehouse.
On the inside, thousands of flashing lights blink and fans whirr as rows of computer servers power AI.
While some are built by tech giants like Amazon, other developers claim commercial sensitivities when asked what they are actually powering.
Scotland's centres are currently quite small, but some of proposals for the hyperscale versions are immense.
One of the biggest is at Auchtertool in Fife.
The site would span 60 hectares (150 acres) - about the size of 84 football pitches.
What's the controversy?
AI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.
But Scotland's data centre debate is not really about the technology inside the building - it's about the scale and impact of the centres themselves.
At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie, which has a capacity for 12MW.
The new data centres being proposed are a whole new level.
If one planned for Chapelcross in Dumfries and Galloway goes ahead, it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world.
At Auchtertool, the planned 600MW data centre would be the same size as the neighbouring village.
Other concerns focus on:
- their size and impact on the landscape
- the amount of electricity they require
- the water needed to cool equipment
- noise generated by thousands of servers and cooling systems
The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies.
The Scottish government has so far refused to impose a moratorium.
Why build them in Scotland?
One of Scotland's biggest selling points for data centre developers is its strong renewable energy sector.
Scotland generates huge amounts of electricity from wind, and some of that power is currently wasted because the grid does not have enough capacity to move it from where it is produced to where it is needed.
However, experts caution that this does not mean data centres would run entirely on renewable energy.
During periods of low wind or when clouds are blocking the sun, it may mean having to fire up fossil fuel power stations to provide the energy required to keep the servers blinking.
Don't data centres use a lot of water?
As well as using huge amounts of electricity, the giant data centres can require large quantities of water to prevent them from overheating.
While the tech industry says it is developing more efficient cooling systems, industry sources told the BBC last year the UK government's plan to make the UK a "world leader" in AI could put already stretched supplies of drinking water under strain.
An expert recently claimed that Scotland's current data centres use less water each day than its libraries, but there are significant concerns over what the water consumption could be if any of the hyperscale centres were given the go-ahead.
And what about the hum?
Data centres have many fans cooling down the servers inside and people in the US who live near them have reported hearing a constant noise, with concerns it has also driven away wildlife.
What are the potential benefits of data centres?
As well as having a stake in a key future technology, those behind AI data centres say they will create jobs.
Lanarkshire has been designated an AI growth zone by the UK government, with data centres at its heart.
When it was announced in January, external, Â£8bn of investment and 3,400 jobs were promised.
The type of jobs a data centre creates has also been debated.
About 800 are expected to be in AI, with 50 apprenticeships. The rest are in construction.
Apatura - the developer behind 10 of the hyperscale data centre proposals in Scotland - highlights its green credentials with its access to renewable energy and battery storage.
What are the politics behind it?
With China and the US hoping to win the AI race, the UK government does not want to be left behind.
The Scottish government also supports the investment in the AI growth zone.
In August, it announced that ministers would have to be notified of proposed centres over 50MW in capacity.
A month later, it rejected the Scottish Greens' call for applications to be paused until new national guidelines are in force.
However, it said environmental impact assessments would have to be submitted.
The government also said it was "highly unlikely" any large data centres would be given the green light before Christmas, and promised that new guidance would be published by the festive season.

President Donald Trump has championed sprawling health policy changes under the Make America Healthy Again movement, but a KFF-Associated Press survey of rural voters found people aren’t seeing the initiatives reach their communities.
More than a year into President Donald Trump’s sweeping immigration crackdown, a poll finds that voters in rural parts of the country are divided on whether those immigration policies have benefited or harmed their communities.
In the Associated Press-KFF survey of more than 2,000 rural voters in August, about a third said the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement had been positive for their community and about a third said it had been negative. The remaining 3 in 10, roughly, said it had no impact.
Trump promised tough enforcement on the campaign trail in 2024, and the survey highlights how a cornerstone of his base, rural supporters of his Make America Great Again movement, are especially likely to say they see a benefit where they live from the Republican president’s stringent immigration policies.
Yet many rural voters also say immigrants are a key part of their local economies, and some believe Trump’s immigration actions have gone too far.
Laura Leigh Taylor, a 37-year-old farmer who voted for Trump in 2024, said she disapproves of the wide-ranging scope of Trump’s immigration crackdown, which resulted in a friend’s hardworking father being deported.
“I understand getting rid of the rapists and the murderers,” she said. “But all the people that fell in between, that really weren’t doing nothing but taking care of their family, … they got torn from their families.”
Taylor now regrets her vote for Trump. As a resident of Smithville, Georgia, a town of about 600, Taylor thinks she will vote for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in November because, she said, the Democrats have been the ones talking about families being uprooted by Trump’s immigration enforcement.
“Just because of that simple fact, I’m going to go with him,” Taylor said.
Most Rural Voters Want Politicians To Talk About Immigration
Roughly three-quarters of rural voters say it’s “extremely” or “very” important for midterm candidates to talk about immigration, though that’s lower than the share who want them to address the cost of living, fraud in government programs, or healthcare costs.
Rural voters don’t overwhelmingly think Trump’s immigration policies have helped their communities, but they are also less likely than the general public to say that Trump has overstepped in his efforts, which have involved mass deportations and rapid deportations of immigrants to countries where they have no ties.
Only about 4 in 10 rural voters say Trump has “gone too far” in restricting legal immigration or deporting immigrants living in the U.S. without authorization, below the 55% of U.S. adults overall who said the same in a September AP-NORC poll.
John Thomas, a 55-year-old from Liberty, Kentucky, supports Trump’s efforts to deport people without legal status. Thomas, who has just been approved for disability benefits after injuring his back in 2008, believes they put too much of a burden on the healthcare system. Regulating immigration, he said, is a means of providing better healthcare to Americans.
“They’ve been taking from everybody,” Thomas said of immigrants. “People that really need this stuff can’t get it because of them.”
David Grabowski, a professor of healthcare policy at Harvard Medical School, said that research suggests immigrants use less healthcare than native-born Americans. “It is hard to argue that they are placing an undue burden on the system,” he said, because many immigrants work in healthcare and pay taxes.
Most Rural Voters See Immigrants’ Economic Importance
Immigrants often play key roles in sustaining local industries, including by filling jobs in manufacturing, healthcare, and agriculture. The survey suggests the vast majority of rural voters see immigrants in the country legally as an important part of their local economies.
Shannon Monnat, director of the Center for Policy Research at Syracuse University and president of the Rural Sociological Society, said immigration has been a demographic lifeline for much of rural America. Rural areas have been losing young adults for years, she said.
“For a lot of small towns, immigrants are the reason the school and hospital stayed open and the county didn’t shrink,” Monnat said.
About 7 in 10 rural voters see immigrants who are in the country legally as “very” or “somewhat” important to their local economies, and a similar share say the same about temporary or seasonal agriculture workers. Hundreds of thousands of immigrants take seasonal jobs on U.S. farms each year, with most of them coming from Mexico, on H-2A visas.
Rural voters with a connection to agriculture and farming are more likely than those without one to say that temporary or seasonal workers are “very important” to their local economies, the poll found.
Jeff Miller, a 56-year-old Republican hydro blaster and vacuum technician, has mostly been pleased with Trump’s agenda, and he believes things are “heading in the right direction.” The one thing Miller has struggled with is Trump’s aggressive immigration policy, which he blames for the deportation of a “really good worker” and friend, who was removed from the U.S. when his work permit expired.
Miller, from Racine, Ohio, said he would support exceptions for hard workers, or just a less aggressive approach.
“There’s kind of an up-and-down thing because I lost a really good friend over that,” Miller said.

a4faf2fd12d9.text: The Supreme Court 's next chapter begins Monday, with the justices set to decide key questions involving President Trump's immigration agenda, climate -change litigation and gun control in their new term. The big picture: But one of the most closely watched fights may be on Truth Social, rather than the docket, as an increasingly agitated Trump chastises the high court he helped shape. The executive and judicial branches are set for another round in the white-columned ring with a president who moves at breakneck speed . State of play: The court recently agreed to hear two major immigration cases, one over mandatory detention for certain immigrants and another over deporting immigrants to third countries where they lack ties. On the latter, the high court allowed the administration to restart its fast-tracked third-country deportations late last month while it considers the underlying legal questions in December. The court agreed Thursday to take up the detention case, setting the stage to test the Trump administration's legal interpretation that noncitizens who entered the country illegally, but have been living in the U.S., are to be held without bond. While federal appeals courts have been divided on the issue, a vast majority — nine of the 11 — have rejected the Trump administration's interpretation. Flashback: While the Supreme Court shot down Trump's attempt to undermine birthright citizenship last term, it handed him a number of immigration wins and green-lit policies on its shadow docket. Those victories for Trump allowed the administration to end temporary protected status , enforce stricter asylum rules and use a revamped tool to check voters' citizenship . Zoom out: Before those cases come to the bench, the court will hear arguments Monday in a key climate case that could determine the fate of state-court lawsuits nationwide seeking climate damages from oil giants, Axios' Ben Geman reports. The court also added two other cases to its lineup Thursday, on top of the mandatory detention debate: One is about a federal law protecting land use by religious groups brought by a missionary organization, and the other is about military benefits in divorce settlement agreements. Later this year, the court will weigh the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style weapons and consider whether Arizona can mandate proof of citizenship for people registering to vote. More disputes over other Trump policies are sure to reach the court this term. Friction point: Though the high court has inflated executive power and gave the president a number of summer shadow docket wins, it also checked some of his most audacious actions last term. He didn't like that. After the justices blocked the administration's pre-midterm attempt to rewrite mail-in voting rules, the president raged against his own Supreme Court picks. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves," he wrote on Truth Social. In a recent interview with Time, the president said he regretted nominating them, saying, "I gave them the chance of a lifetime, and it's unfortunate what they did." There is new cause for alarm in the Horn of Africa. A week after a coalition of seven opposition groups announced an alliance to overthrow the government of Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, fighting has broken out across several regions of the country of 130 million people. Led by the Tigrayan Peopleâs Liberation Front, the militias of Ethiopiaâs largest regions of Amhara and Oromia have also pledged their support.
Early battles have taken place along a critical commercial route leading east to the port of Djibouti, while drone strikes were carried out around the armyâs main airbase near the capital, Addis Ababa. The choice of economic and political targets reflects the reality that even though the Tigrayans are weaker militarily than in their previous war that ended in 2022, they can still create asymmetric pressure on the government.
Ethiopiaâs army is now quickly regrouping and is pushing the TPLF back into Tigray, where government forces have retaken the regional airport and now occupy the capital, Mekelle. As the conflict moves into urban areas, the risk of displacement and civilian casualties grows. And in a region already suffering from aid shortages, and anticipating even greater food insecurity from this yearâs El Nino, humanitarians are rightly nervous about a potential catastrophic fallout.
But the Tigrayans and their âAlliance for Survivalâ allies believe they have an ace up their sleeves. A coalition of neighboring states, led by Egypt and including Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia have reportedly been working in the background to support the Prime Ministerâs armed opponents. Abiyâs announcement of building three new hydroelectric dams on the Nile, along with his threatening claims on the Eritrean port of Assab, and his armyâs support for the Rapid Support Forces militia next door in Sudan have made him no friends across the region. All would like to see his ambitions contained.
With a fully internationalized conflict already raging in neighboring Sudan and long-time foe Eritrea poised to enter the fight on the side of the Tigrayans, the risk that Ethiopiaâs conflict converges with existing regional instability and animosities is high. The fallout from a regional war on US priorities from counterterrorism to Red Sea security would be disastrous, which raises the question why isnât the Trump Administration doing more to stop it?
On Oct. 4, the State Department urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to âexercise maximum restraint,â though curiously did not address the current fighting by Ethiopiaâs internal armed groups. But back in June, the State Department sanctioned a group of Tigrayan officials for âundermining resolution to the crisis in Tigrayâ and last week the US ambassador in Addis blamed Tigrayans for their âpoor decision to launch a large-scale offensive.â None of this suggests an even-handed approach this time around that would enable Washington to mediate an end to the violence as it did in 2022 to end the last Tigray war. This time, Washington has picked a side.
Rubioâs newfound prioritization of commercial diplomacy, reflected in the announcement last week of the sale of $5 billion in Boeing aircraft to Ethiopiaâs national airline, speaks to Washingtonâs focus on economic returns over peacemaking. But that view is shortsighted.
Ethiopiaâs double-digit economic growth and large infrastructure plans are vulnerable to the threat of nationwide war and regional meddling. The African Union has called for calm, but only Washington has the political leverage to manage a regional crisis. With Red Sea instability occupying more of Washingtonâs strategic focus, it would do well to prioritize peacemaking and ensure that Ethiopiaâs economic potential is not undone by a descent into a region-wide conflict.
Cameron Hudson is an independent analyst focused on African peace, security and governance. He previously worked on Africa at the CIA, State Department and the US National Security Council.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called an early election for 29 November after recent defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.
Speculation about a snap election had been building over the weekend after parliament rejected two decree laws put forward by the minority government to protect tenants in the rental market.
The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after she was unable to afford a sharp rent rise has sparked nationwide protests and increased pressure for housing reform.
In a televised address on Monday, SÃ¡nchez said that to push reforms through he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites".
Housing has not been the only issue causing problems for SÃ¡nchez's leadership in recent months, with his party having been caught up in numerous corruption scandals and facing pressure on other cost-of-living issues and immigration.
"We have made mistakes and have not achieved everything we had set out to do," SÃ¡nchez said, acknowledging there were still "a lot of problems to solve, particularly in the areas of inequality, of public services and access to housing".
SÃ¡nchez's left-wing coalition government is made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, and does not have a majority in parliament.
Spain was not due to hold a general election until the summer of 2027 at the latest.
SÃ¡nchez has been prime minister since June 2018. His Socialist party finished second in the last election, in 2023.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, it fell short of a majority.
SÃ¡nchez remained in power after striking agreements with left-wing parties and securing support from Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.
Speaking after Monday's announcement, the leader of the People's Party, Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o, said: "At last, Spaniards will be able to decide".
The opposition leader said it would not be "just another election", but a chance for voters to choose between "decline or change, lies or change, incompetence or change, division or change, corruption or change".
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people took to the streets in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona, calling for greater protections for tenants.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis when she was forcibly evicted from her Madrid home on 23 September.
A legal glitch allowed her landlord to raise her rent from â¬500 (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650. It was later lowered to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than her monthly pension.
She was removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years, and was later admitted to hospital.
Her lawyer has since said she will be able to return to her home, but the incident has prompted widespread anger over housing.
The left-wing coalition government responded with two decree laws in an effort to defuse the protests.
The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".
The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas.
The political right argued the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Juan Bravo of the People's Party said last week "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".
SÃ¡nchez's leadership has been marred by numerous corruption scandals in recent months.
In April, his wife BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez was charged with corruption after a two-year criminal investigation.
She is accused of using her relationship to advance her private career - allegations she denies, and which have been dismissed by SÃ¡nchez as a right-wing attempt to undermine his coalition.
In May, police raided the Socialist party's headquarters in Madrid as part of an investigation into allegations an operative was paid to carry out a misinformation campaign. The party has denied the allegations.
And in June, SÃ¡nchez's former transport minister, JosÃ© Luis Ãbalos, was jailed for 24 years after he was found guilty of being involved in a network that received kickbacks from the sale of face masks during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The Spanish prime minister also came under scrutiny for his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis over the summer, when tens of thousands of people entered the territory from Morocco without authorisation.

A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country.
The "very serious incident" happened in the north-eastern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, FranÃ§ois-Xavier Lauch.
"The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital in nearby.
Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days.
There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury.
Regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord reported that they lost their hand after picking up a police stun grenade.
Officials have not yet provided details.
A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened".
The incident took place close to the Auguste BÃ©hal high school, the prefect said.
Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school.
"At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media.
"Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred."
The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on.
"In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment."

Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe, after the US withdrew all of its bombers from the military base.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed, which follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
A Number 10 spokesperson said he would not comment on "foreign nations' military operations", but said the base was safe, and pointed to US President Donald Trump's comments last week, where he "praised our police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.
He added that Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had said last week, "we have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world".
RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - is at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.
Earlier on Monday, the New York Times reported US commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford according to two US officials.
The newspaper wrote the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours.
Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

Abu Dhabiâs XRG is backing Argentinaâs bid to become a major liquefied natural gas exporter. ADNOCâs international arm agreed in June to take a 32% stake in three Argentine gas blocks. They will feed the countryâs first LNG export terminal, designed to produce 12 million tons a year in its initial phase. âNo country or company secures its energy future alone,â Executive Chairman Sultan Al Jaber said in Paris last week.
At a time when exports from their home markets have been severely constrained, such international investments are only increasing in importance, helping Gulf producers meet customer demand and benefit from higher prices.
