170b9fc8efe7.text: By — Hillel Italie, Associated Press Hillel Italie, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-francis-diaries-to-be-published-next-month-revealing-reflections-on-vatican-years Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Francis' diaries to be published next month, revealing reflections on Vatican years World Oct 5, 2026 1:33 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Journal entries kept by Pope Francis before and during his papacy will be published this fall for the first time. Image, an imprint of Penguin Random House Christian Publishing Group, announced Monday that "The Private Diary of Pope Francis" will be released in English and four other languages on Nov. 24. According to Image, the book will provide an "extraordinary glimpse" into the late pontiff's "hopes and fears, struggles and prayers." It will be issued in partnership with Libreria Editrice Vaticana, or LEV, the Vatican Publishing House. The writings span from December 1992, just over two decades before he became pope, to August 2024, eight months before he died and was succeeded by Pope Leo XIV. The English-language edition of his private reflections was translated from the Spanish original by Sister Bernadette Reis and edited and annotated by Víctor Manuel Fernández, an Argentine cardinal who heads the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith. READ MORE: Pope Leo meets LGBTQ+ Catholic advocate and vows continuity with Pope Francis' legacy of welcome Born Jorge Mario Bergoglio, Francis was a native of Argentina and history's first Latin American pope. He was known for his down-to-earth style and emphasis on humility, including visits to poor countries with persecuted Christian minorities rather than the traditional strongholds of Catholicism. At the start of the coronavirus pandemic, from an empty St. Peter's Square, he called for "all of us to row together, each of us in need of comforting the other." At times, he was controversial. He angered some conservatives with his outreach to LGBTQ+ Catholics and was widely criticized for saying that those who accused Chilean Bishop Juan Barros of helping to protect the alleged pedophile Rev. Fernando Karadima had committed slander. In 2016, commenting on then-presidential candidate Donald Trump's vow to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexican border, Francis said that anyone building a wall to keep migrants out "is not Christian." In his lifetime, Francis' books included "The Name of God Is Mercy" and the memoir "Hope." He died on April 21, 2025 at the age of 88. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The Defense Ministry said late Sunday that recent strikes on refineries in cities, including Moscow, Yaroslavl, Ust-Luga, Perm, Saratov and Syzran, had disabled 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity. The claim could not be independently verified. Moscow and Kyiv have intensified their aerial assaults as progress along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line has largely ground to a halt. Ukrainian strikes cause fuel issues in Russia Ukraine has launched repeated attacks on refineries from Moscow to Siberia, sparking a widespread fuel crisis in Russia earlier this year that forced authorities to restrict gasoline sales. Russian officials have not released figures on damage to the country's oil infrastructure. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes' economic impact, President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 1 that they had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product. "They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy. Did they achieve their goal? Partially," Putin told a meeting of the Valdai Club forum of international foreign policy experts. Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said analysts from Ukraine's intelligence services, the General Staff and the Defense Ministry had assessed the strikes' effects. "Fifty-one percent of struck refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy's economy, to its ability to carry out aggression and supply its troop groupings. Our deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory," he said. Russia has historically been the world's third-largest producer of refined fuel products from crude, after the U.S. and China. Some of Russia's 32 refineries have been hit as many as 15 times since the start of the war, and one refinery has been hit every three days in recent months, creating a cycle of damage and emergency repairs that could degrade units long term, according to the International Energy Agency. Ukrainian strikes have also increasingly targeted the more complex equipment that removes impurities from fuel, which takes months to repair. The IEA says diesel output has fallen by about 30%, and drivers have had to wait up to 40 hours to fill up at gasoline stations. Russian refiners have tried to compensate by delaying scheduled maintenance and bringing mothballed units back online. Another response has been to lower fuel quality standards to maintain gasoline supplies, which risks damage to engines and pollution control equipment. The Kremlin has also banned diesel exports, pushing global prices higher and prompting U.S. President Donald Trump on Sept. 13 to urge Ukraine to stop hitting refineries. "There may be people under the rubble of the residential building that was hit. A search and rescue operation is underway," Terekhov wrote on his Telegram channel. An earlier Russian drone attack on the city's Industrialnyi district also killed one person, Terekhov said late Sunday. Vehicles and an administrative building were set alight and apartment buildings were damaged, he said. Another person was also killed in a separate Russian attack on the Sloviansk community in Ukraine's Donetsk region, said Vadym Liakh, head of the Sloviansk city military administration. He urged residents not to wait for a mandatory evacuation order but to leave the area. READ MORE: Russian drones hammer apartments and cultural landmark in Ukraine, killing 7 Ukraine's air force reported that Russia launched 205 drones overnight into Monday, with 172 shot down or suppressed. Russia's Defense Ministry said in a statement on Monday that it had struck an electrical substation in the Kharkiv region, in addition to energy and port infrastructure and maritime vessels used by Ukraine's military elsewhere in the country. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian drone attack caused a fire on board a commercial vessel that later sank in the Black Sea. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said. In a post on X on Monday, Zelenskyy described the attack as "a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel" in neutral waters. He said the vessel was Turkish-owned and carrying corn. Russia did not immediately comment on the incident. Ukraine has struggled in recent weeks to fend off Russia's intensified aerial attacks on cities that include ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones. The onslaught aims to terrorize civilians, officials and analysts say, and break their will to resist Russia's full-scale invasion since 2022. President Donald Trump has said the US moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US had known of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers.
Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.
So urgent had the departure been that some of the planes left before refuelling aircraft could be arranged to support them, US officials who wished to remain anonymous told the New York Times.
"So, what you saw there is the secretary of war [Pete Hegseth], out of an abundance of caution, trying to protect our guys," Vice-President JD Vance said as he left Washington for a trip to Alaska.
Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
While speaking to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.
Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.
"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."
Washington, he added, "actually knows the people that made the threat", he but did not confirm who.
The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.
One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb - a covert drone attack on five Russian bases in June last year - as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance.
"Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said.
Trump's comments, and those of Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world.
RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Following the release of the first five men, Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident.
Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.
He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."
Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident.
Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".
Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
The redeployment from RAF Fairford will reduce America's capacity to "quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat", Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute, was quoted as saying by Reuters news agency.
However, the use of the base had already been limited given London's stipulation that it should only be used for defensive strikes, he added.
The planes could potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for air-to-air refuelling but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, Bergs added.

France is braced for major protests on Tuesday, after organisers called for a nationwide day of action in support of students demanding more investment in education.
It comes after a week of demonstrations, which saw students blockading hundreds of schools, at least 190 students injured, and more than 5,000 people arrested.
One student had his hand blown off during a confrontation on Monday, while another was reportedly struck in the head by a tear gas grenade last week.
France's prime minister said the government had announced measures to address their demands, but the Union Syndicale LycÃ©enne (USL), a major organiser of the protests, said the government had offered "nothing concrete".
The organisation called on people to join their mobilisation on Tuesday in the face of "this political deadlock and what we describe as unprecedented repression of the movement".
Some other organisations have also shown their support for the students, with the teachers' union SNES-FSU urging its members to join Tuesday's protest.
The radical-left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a year of major unrest, which saw millions of workers go on strike.
The wave of demonstrations began in September in Paris and has spread across the country, with students protesting over a range of issues, including overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings, and a lack of teachers.
The protests were started by high school students, who were later joined by university students.
On Sunday, French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu announced a series of measures to "address the difficulties faced by secondary school students and education staff", promising "visible changes" in schools.
However, he also said: "We will make no concessions to violence. We stand by students and staff who have been assaulted, as well as police officers and gendarmes who have been injured."
The unrest has not only seen schools blockaded, but also rubbish bins set on fire. Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "burned and ransacked" since the start of the protests.
Violent clashes between students and the police have led to some serious injuries throughout the course of the protests so far.
On Monday, a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation near a school in the northern city of Lens. The student was transferred to a nearby hospital and his injury is not life-threatening, according to officials.
Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'AumÃ´ne after reportedly being struck on the head by a tear gas grenade.
The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer.
Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered".
"It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying.
"This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."
Among the 5,060 people arrested since the start of the movement, 87% were minors and 13% were adults, according to France's justice ministry, external.
Fourteen people have reportedly been placed in pre-trial detention, while 1,802 people are facing prosecution, including 319 adults and 1,483 minors.
The USL has accused police of using excessive force against the protesters. Responding to this allegation last week, Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said the demonstrations had been policed in "an extremely proportionate manner".
While France's next presidential election is still months away, the protests and the response by French authorities have been heavily politicised.
The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for fuelling the protests. Lecornu said LFI was being "irresponsible" in calling for the movement to expand.
The leader of the hard-right National Rally, Marine Le Pen, has also criticised the left for its response.
"This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organised by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise," she said, calling for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.
Meanwhile MÃ©lenchon, the LFI's party's presidential candidate, has been blaming the police for "abuses of power", calling on people to take to the streets to "protect the youth demonstrations".
The left-wing mayor of Marseille, BenoÃ®t Payan, condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves calmly, he said.

Armed Border Patrol agents raided a protest camp in Lochiel, in southeast Arizona, making way for contractors to cut down the last standing cottonwood tree Monday morning for a double border wall, after protesters protected it for more than 70 days.
Activists in Lochiel said at least 12 people had been arrested as of 8 a.m. during the ongoing raid. Border Patrol agents ignored demands for a warrant as they entered the private property and destroyed tents, according to news releases from activist groups on the ground.
Dubbed the “grandmother tree,” the cottonwood cut down Monday was hundreds of years old. It was one of several that lined the edge of private property along Border Road, a dirt road that runs along the U.S.-Mexico border, in a remote area of Arizona in the San Rafael Valley about 25 miles east of Nogales.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection said Monday in a statement to Arizona Luminaria that it has now removed all four cottonwood trees on federal land in Lochiel that were marked for removal.
“CBP recognizes the importance of protecting the environment, wildlife, and cultural resources during border wall construction,” the statement said. “While concerns exist about impacts to sensitive areas, it is important to note that illegal immigration itself poses significant environmental challenges. High volumes of unauthorized crossings often result in substantial amounts of trash, pollution, and damage to natural resources, including sensitive habitats and agriculture.”
CBP did not answer additional questions from Arizona Luminaria about how many protesters were arrested or what charges they face.
After three cottonwoods were cut down in June, activists set up a tree-sit in an attempt to protect the last remaining grandmother tree. At least one person sat or slept in the tree at all times. For 71 days, people camped out in private property just north of the tree and took turns occupying it.
On Monday around 6:30 a.m., Border Patrol agents with their faces covered began to arrest protesters, videos posted on Instagram show. People screamed and some warned the agents that they were pushing people into barbed wire on the ground. The protesters were trying to move back onto the private property on the other side of the barbed wire.
“You’re stepping on them!” a person is heard screaming.
“You’re pushing them into barbed wire!” someone else yells at the agents.
Another video shot from a distance shows the giant tree falling over as people scream and cry.
Life at the Camp
Kate Scott, co-founder of Madrean Archipelago Wildlife Center, was the first to notice contractors were cutting down the cottonwoods this summer. After speaking to a worker in June, and learning their plans to cut down all the trees, she gathered support and started sitting out near the tree. Eventually, with the support of Indigenous activists, the protesters in Lochiel started a morning prayer ritual. Every morning the group would hold a sunrise prayer for the land, Scott said. It was during that prayer ceremony that Border Patrol agents raided the camp on Monday.
When Arizona Luminaria visited the camp on Sept. 23, it was a quiet day at the protest camp, with only one or two Border Patrol vehicles driving through the area. As of late morning, there was no construction happening near the camp. But months earlier, when the protest first started, construction workers would arrive around 3 a.m. and work all morning, Scott said.
“This was a very, very intense place,” she said, adding that the sound of the machinery would wake them in the early hours.
About a quarter mile east of where the tree once stood, two rows of 30-foot tall border panels on either side of the road came to a sudden stop. A stack of panels on the road sat between the two walls and another stack of panels sat a few feet away. The new wall runs east along the rolling hills in this area of the border as far as the eye can see.
On Sept. 14, three protesters wearing bird and jaguar costumes, representing the endangered species in the area, were arrested after entering the construction site.Those arrests encouraged more people from across the country to join the camp, Scott said.
In late September, dozens of tents were scattered along the tall grass inside private property. A group of people were learning to safely climb rope to get onto the wooden plank in the grandmother tree.
Down the road, the group had secured a guest house with a bathroom, a bed and fridges to store food and other belongings. The landowner was renting it out to the group. Scott called it “Casita de la Esperanza,” meaning House of Hope.
Another cottonwood, this one in Mexico, held banners that read, “From MN to MX resistance is fertile,” and “Chinga la Migra.” Four calves rested in the shade inside a pen. For about a week, activists in Mexico held their own tree sit in solidarity with U.S. protesters.
To get to Lochiel, a visitor has to traverse more than 10 miles of rough dirt roads through the Coronado National Forest. It’s a remote ranching town between Nogales and Bisbee, south of Sonoita. Ranch homes are scattered on vast parcels of land. A small white church sits about 100 feet from the border wall, with a large white cross standing on a hill above the church. Where there aren’t 30-foot border panels, a barbed-wire fence about 3 to 4 feet tall marks the border.
Along Border Road, between Casita de la Esperanza and where the last remaining grandmother tree once stood, the trunks of two other cottonwoods lay on the ground after being cut down. There was a third between them, Scott said, but it was dragged up the hill to a “graveyard of grandmothers.”
The two fallen trees were so big they left a 4 foot deep hole in the ground where they were once rooted. Banners activists tied around the trunk remain on the fallen trees. And on one of them, new growth had started to come up, with bright green leaves emerging from the trunk.
This article first appeared on AZ Luminaria and is republish

The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments from oil companies on Monday that could help decide the fate of more than two dozen lawsuits accusing the industry of deceiving the public about climate change. The claims seek potentially billions of dollars in damages to help pay the costs imposed by climate-related extreme weather.
Yet the questions before the court did not focus on the merits of these claims but instead on technical legal matters over whether they should proceed at all.
The case being argued was brought in 2018 by the city and county of Boulder against ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy in Colorado state court. While the case and dozens like it have survived multiple appeals in state and federal courts, the oil companies are asking the Supreme Court to declare that federal law preempts state and local governments from bringing such claims.
“This case represents an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct,” said Kannon Shanmugam, arguing for Exxon and Suncor. In effect, Shanmugam said, Boulder is attempting to use state law to regulate oil company activity around the world. “If Boulder’s claims are allowed to go forward, some 90,000 municipalities across the country would have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil fuel producers.”
But Boulder and dozens of other plaintiffs have argued their claims do not attempt to impose any limits on oil companies at all—the Boulder case seeks damages, not an injunction on any activity.
“This case is not about emissions,” said Kevin Russell, who argued the case for Boulder. “It’s about deception.”
Oil companies and conservative groups have been ramping up a campaign to block the lawsuits from proceeding as they inch closer to trial. Some states have enacted laws barring such lawsuits and Republicans have introduced federal legislation that would shield oil companies from climate liability claims. The Trump administration has also intervened in several state cases, including Boulder’s, to try to block them from moving forward. Many scientists whose work is being cited in the cases have been the subject of more than 100 public records requests from conservative groups seeking information about their work and funders, according to Politico.
The first question that arose at Monday’s hearing, posed by Justice Clarence Thomas, is whether the court has jurisdiction to hear the case at this stage because no ruling has been issued.
The oil companies contend that the proliferating lawsuits are already causing sufficient harm and that the court should decide now whether the cases should proceed. Several justices suggested they thought it might be too early to intervene.
“I think Boulder’s best shot is on the jurisdictional question, whether this case is too early,” Michael Gerrard, faculty director at the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University, said in an interview.
The justices also probed the arguments of whether federal law preempts a state claim about climate change and emissions, either through the Clean Air Act or the Constitution.
Several of the conservative justices seemed inclined to agree that federal law preempts at least some of Boulder’s claims, Gerrard said.

The oil companies’ lawyers have argued that the Clean Air Act preempts any claims against oil companies tied to climate pollution. They also argue that the Constitution itself gives the federal government exclusive control over interstate pollution.
Russell argued that Boulder’s claim does not seek to limit pollution, and that there is nothing in the Clean Air Act or the Constitution that would bar states from taking actions that have a secondary effect of reducing pollution, such as imposing a gas tax or, in this case, seeking damages from oil companies.
Justice Samuel Alito was not at the hearing after recusing himself last week. While Alito gave no explanation for the decision, he had been under pressure to do so because he owns stock in oil companies that are party to other lawsuits that would be affected by the court’s decision.
Alito’s absence leaves open the possibility of a tie vote, which would allow the case to move forward.
Supporters of the case held rallies outside the court calling on the justices to let it proceed.
“Boulder, like other cities and counties across the country, is confronting realities associated with climate change every day, from wildfires and floods to drought, extreme heat, and growing pressures on our water and infrastructure,” said Boulder’s city manager, Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde, in a statement after the hearing. “The legal question before the court is whether taxpayers must bear these costs alone or must the defendants also pay their fair share for the harms they have caused.”
Many conservative groups and politicians have filed briefs supporting the oil companies, and the Trump administration presented arguments to the justices on Monday.
Boulder won supportive briefs from not only climate advocacy groups and Democrats but also many academics and former Environmental Protection Agency officials, including some appointed by Republican presidents.
Many of the cases brought by states and local governments have been paused pending the outcome of the Supreme Court’s ruling in the Boulder case. The decision, expected by the end of the court’s term in June, could bring those claims to an abrupt halt or set the stage for trials to finally begin.

A US man who once appeared on the TV talent competition American Idol has been sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for murdering his wife.
Caleb Flynn, 40, was found guilty last week after a short deliberation by the jury, which rejected his claim that an intruder broke into his Ohio home and shot his wife, Ashley Flynn, as she slept.
He was also found guilty of eight additional charges, including aggravated murder and tampering with evidence.
Letters from his two daughters were read in court during the sentencing hearing on Monday, pleading with him to finally admit his guilt and questioning why he killed their mother.
Flynn, a former music pastor, fatally shot his wife, a 37-year-old teacher, in February before staging their home in Tipp City to appear as if someone had broken in through the garage.
Flynn claims he was asleep when he heard gunshots and found his wife dead in bed after finding the garage door open. Their two children, ages 9 and 11, were also sleeping in the house at the time.
His wife's sister, Kayla Keyt, read a victim impact statement saying the murder had caused his daughters to question their Christian faith and had "shattered a family who trusted you".
One of his daughter's letters read: "Dear Daddy, I don't even know where to start. How could you do such a thing?"
She also said: "Mommy was the perfect person... And then you chose to kill the only mother I ever had."
The other daughter's letter began "Dear Caleb", rather than addressing him as her father, and asked him to "tell everyone what you did it and receive your outcome".
"You made me feel like an idiot thinking I could trust you," his daughter said. She added that she continues to have faith in God, and that she will never visit her father in prison.
Flynn sobbed loudly as the letters from his children were read.
The sentencing hearing also included Flynn reading a statement expressing love for his family, apologising for unspecified "decisions" that he made, and again claiming that he did not kill his wife.
"I made vows to Ashley on our wedding day. I failed those vows," he said.
Judge Jeannine Pratt called Flynn an "extreme" risk to the public as she imposed her sentence.
The murder verdict last week followed eight days of testimony, during which several incriminating text messages Flynn sent to his former mistress, Alleigha Botner, were read out and AI-generated songs were played that prosecutors said he made for her.
Evidence presented during trial included police body camera footage and activity on Flynn's iPhone and Apple Watch from around the time of the murder when he claimed to have been sleeping.
The prosecution also called dozens of witnesses, including Botner, whom he met while she was an intern at his church.
Botner read aloud in court some of their 100,000 text messages, including one where Flynn wrote: "I was up until 4am last night crying, literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail."
In another message, he wrote: "I just want her dead and gone."
Flynn did not testify during the trial, and his defence team called no witnesses.
His lawyer, Patrick Mulligan, has said he plans to file a notice of appeal, telling reporters last week: "There's a lack of evidence on prior calculation and design."
Mulligan argued that evidence of infidelity was not evidence of murder and questioned why Flynn was being accused of tampering with evidence because his gun could not be found.
This gun, which had been kept in the console of his truck, has been missing since investigators arrived at the scene and found the truck's centre console open.
Prosecutor Paul Watkins read a statement from Ashley Flynn's family in court after the verdict in September, saying: "Ashley loved Jesus with her whole heart."
"She loved people," the statement continued. "Most of all, she loved being a Mum."
Flynn briefly appeared on American Idol in 2013, saying that he loved his wife "more than anything".

f6e29287ac6d.text: President Trump said Monday that the United States will help Russia amid a potential case of pneumonic plague , though he hasn't spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin about it. Why it matters: International concern spiked over the weekend over the news that a Russian lab worker had died from a possible case of pneumonic plague, reminding some of how the COVID-19 epidemic began. Trump's comments came after a question about the reported death of Darya Shipilova, who was potentially exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. There has been no official confirmation that Shipilova's death was due to pneumonic plague, but five hospitals in the area and dozens of institute workers have been quarantined out of precaution. Russian health authorities say Shipilova died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing showed no pathogen tied to her work. No additional deaths or sicknesses tied to the incident have been reported. What they're saying: "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday. "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can." Trump said the disease used to be more controllable, but "microbes and the germs have gotten stronger." The president appeared to be referring to antimicrobial resistance , but pneumonic plague itself remains treatable with antibiotics when diagnosed early Between the lines: The White House is monitoring the outbreak, Axios scooped, with the Department of Health and Human Services and State Department also on alert. The European Commission is also "very closely" monitoring the suspected outbreak. Go deeper: How pneumonic plague spreads, and how it is and isn't like COVID

The Scoop
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York has been visiting big banks to review their loans to private credit firms and understand their exposure to a financial industry that has unnerved investors and global policymakers.
Fed officials have gone into JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Barclays, and Morgan Stanley since the spring with questions about overall exposure, risk-management, and collateral quality, people familiar with the matter said.
The Fed, JPMorgan, Barclays, Wells Fargo and Morgan Stanley declined to comment.
The review was prompted in part by JPMorganâs move in March to mark down large swaths of loans in private credit portfolios, particularly those to software companies threatened by AI, the people said. The Fed has concluded its review of some of the banks, including JPM, said the people.
Itâs not uncommon for the Fed to go into banks to review their holdings, particularly when there are frequent headlines about potential risks. The Fed also does regular on-site evaluations and continually surveys for banksâ risks.
Know More
Private-credit firms are one of the fastest-growing borrower sets for banks, which were chased out of risky lending after the 2008 crisis but have since found their way back into the trade by lending to the firms that replaced them. Loans to nonbank institutions have risen from $300 billion in 2016 to more than $1.5 trillion according to FDIC data, and now account for 11% of all bank loans outstanding.
Those loans are backed by private-credit firmsâ own loans, a debt pile that has unnerved regulators. The European Central Bank also recently expanded a probe into private credit, looking at banks with exposures to the market. Last week, the Securities and Exchange Commission released a rare statement about fair value in private assets, serving as a reminder to lenders that they should be rigorous in their valuations and disclosures.
The Bank of England, during its September Financial Policy Committee meeting, said that private credit could be vulnerable to worsening financial conditions after testing the resilience of private markets.
The private credit market got slammed earlier this year when investors panicked about fundsâ exposures to software companies, which suddenly seemed obsolete amid developments in AI. The concerns caused investors in certain types of funds to pull out their money at record rates â sometimes requesting nearly 40% of a single fund in a quarter, but most funds have capped at 5%.
Private credit lenders have long been criticized for the way they value their loans, or mark them, in particular when there is disparity between where different lenders value the same loan and when a companyâs underperformance fails to translate to their marks. But lenders utilize third-party evaluators to create the marks and say they are making careful investments.
Redemption rates have declined at many of the private-credit firms and some investors have warmed to software deals again, as more of them find avenues to finance themselves both in and out of the private credit market.

07c2d66ff4db.text: By — Gerald Imray, Associated Press Gerald Imray, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/laotian-man-deported-by-u-s-to-eswatini-is-released-after-more-than-a-year-in-prison Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Laotian man deported by U.S. to Eswatini is released after more than a year in prison World Oct 5, 2026 4:01 PM EDT CAPE TOWN, South Africa (AP) — A Laotian citizen deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration's immigration crackdown was released from a maximum-security prison in the African nation on Sunday after being held there for more than a year, his lawyer said. Phone Chomsavanh was among five immigrants deported to Eswatini — where he has no ties — in July 2025 in the early days of the Trump administration's secretive and highly contentious third-country deportation program. READ MORE: Supreme Court lets Trump continue deporting people to 3rd countries while justices consider policy Chomsavanh's U.S.-based lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said in a statement announcing his release that he had only been informed that he was being deported to Eswatini shortly before a military cargo plane carrying him and other deportees landed there more than 14 months ago. Chomsavanh was now being deported to Laos, Nguyen said. Chomsavanh and the four other immigrants he was deported to Eswatini with were convicted of serious crimes in the U.S., but had served their sentences by the time they were sent to the Matsapha Correctional Complex near Eswatini's administrative capital, Mbabane. "He had already served his time. Instead they put him on a plane without telling him where it was headed and left him in a prison in a country he had never heard of, where nobody ever accused him of anything," Nguyen said. "He sat there for more than a year. No notice, no hearing, no chance to object. That is not due process by any definition." He said in separate messages to The Associated Press that Chomsavanh had left Eswatini and landed in Johannesburg en route to Laos. An Eswatini government spokesperson didn't immediately acknowledge Chomsavanh's release. Chomsavanh was born in a refugee camp in Thailand after his parents fled Laos, and his family moved to the United States when he was 7, his lawyer said. Chomsavanh is one of around 500 immigrants who have been deported from the United States to African countries that aren't their home nations since the third-country program began last year, according to advocacy groups Human Rights First and Refugees International, which have been monitoring the deportations. Around a dozen African countries have accepted third-country deportees from the U.S., some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments. Eswatini, which is Africa's last absolute monarchy and is ruled by a king, was paid $5.1 million by the Trump administration to take deportees, according to the agreement between the countries. Eswatini has received around 30 deportees so far. The program, which results in immigrants being held in countries they have no ties to and where they haven't been charged with any crime, has been fiercely criticized by rights groups and lawyers. It has been the subject of legal challenges in the U.S. and in some of the countries where immigrants have been sent. The Trump administration has defended the policy as a way to quickly remove immigrants who have final deportation orders from the U.S. when their home countries might not immediately take them back. Last month, a U.S. appeals court upheld a judge's ruling to halt the program, because it didn't give immigrants facing removal from the U.S. time to challenge their deportation to a third country if they fear persecution or torture there. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled last week to temporarily allow U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to continue swiftly removing immigrants to third countries, though it will hear arguments in the case in December. The program has largely been carried out in secrecy, with little transparency over how many immigrants have been deported to third countries, and where and in what conditions they are being held. The US says it is closely monitoring the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was concern the incident could have led to the spread of pneumonic plague, but that there was no cause for alarm.
Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said that "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples".
Unconfirmed reports had suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague is found naturally among wild rodents.
No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since her death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor.
The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead.
Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution.
Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature.
"If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that."
The woman who died, whose first name was given by Russian media as Daria and who was in her late twenties, had recently visited the Buryatia region on the border with Mongolia.
The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis, external, which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death, is found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, external was founded just over 100 years ago.
Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics.
"Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said.
He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here."
"People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said.
"It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it."
Asked if the pathogen might have been studied for potential use as a bio-weapon, the scientist agreed it was possible.
"Because this is Russia people's thoughts are running to that, but I think my earlier explanation is probably more likely," Clarke said.

75b5ef265e81.text: States are taking on the stubbornly high fuel prices squeezing Americans ahead of the midterm elections , pushing through tax holidays and other tactics to offer relief while federal efforts have stalled. Why it matters: With November 3 less than 30 days away, the political stakes of those price-lowering levers — even if the relief is only modest — are surging amid sky-high costs. While several lawmakers have introduced legislation aimed at or pressed for suspending the federal gas tax, which is 18.4 cents per gallon for gas and 24.4 for diesel, Washington hasn't coalesced around a solution. Driving the news: That's left states seeking ways to give their residents relief. Case in point: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) signed a bill last week that suspends Ohio's gas tax for 90 days, an effort that earned bipartisan backing. There's an underlying election story: The state's Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Amy Acton, had called for a gas tax holiday, followed by her rival, Vivek Ramaswamy, announcing a plan with GOP leaders. Flashback: Georgia was the first state to suspend its fuel taxes amid the war in Iran, with Republican Gov. Brian Kemp approving a 60-day pause back in March. Since then, at least five other states (including Ohio), have suspended, lowered or stopped increases in their fuel taxes. Kemp declared a state of emergency in late September and suspended the excise tax again for 30 days. Utah cut its gas tax by some 15% through the end of the year. Gov. Andy Beshear (D-Ky.) froze an expected increase in the gas and diesel taxes in May. Illinois suspended its set increase this summer for six months. Indiana Gov. Mike Braun (R) also suspended Indiana's gas tax in April. He renewed the suspension in late September and lifted restrictions on dyed diesel for farmers and timber harvesters. Friction point: The Trump administration signaled openness to a gas tax holiday this spring, but Congress must suspend the levy. While the idea has been floated before, lawmakers have never done so. Suspending the taxes can bring some relief to consumers, but it wouldn't offset the spikes they've felt at the pump since the start of the war. Plus, critics note doing so could increase the deficit and hurt the Highway Trust Fund it fuels. But as Axios' Ben Geman noted back in May, political winds aren't always predictable — especially with drivers and truckers still feeling the strain months later, and as political messages cluster around cost-of-living concerns. Zoom out: Other states have taken a similar approach to Braun by waiving seasonal and traditional restrictions for strained industries. For example, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey (R) directed state law enforcement to stop enforcing rules against dyed diesel, usually reserved for off-road machinery and exempt from taxes, "to relieve the state's agricultural and timber communities." Louisiana , Nebraska , North Carolina , Oklahoma and Texas took similar action. Still, other states pursued different avenues for relief: California recently took action to permit cheaper, winter-blend gas to be sold earlier than usual, while Michigan allowed gas stations to sell lower-cost gasoline earlier this spring. The bottom line: Even if a federal gas tax holiday remains unlikely, pump pain — and perhaps, the possibility of future political pain — is fueling state action. Tillis says his vote for Hegseth was 'biggest regret of my career' in new book Politics Oct 5, 2026 3:40 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican Sen. Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the "biggest regret of my career" and that he also "should've stopped" Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump's second term. READ MORE: Republican North Carolina Sen. Tillis won't seek reelection after opposing Trump's bill In "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents," to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be "the lone voice in the wilderness" preventing Trump's nominees from confirmation. But he makes clear he was always skeptical about allegations about Hegseth's turbulent management style, treatment of women and excessive drinking — all of which Hegseth denied. "I know for a fact that there are others like me," Tillis writes, "Republicans who agreed to go along with the early demands of the Trump team no matter how ridiculous they were, believing that failing to do so would mean the end of their political career, and who now see that things have gone way too far." He writes that he can count at least 30 of his GOP colleagues who have "expressed reservations (to put it mildly) about many of the president's actions in private. Then, when the reporters showed up with their cameras and microphones, they'd have nothing but nice things to say." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Tillis, who announced last year that he would not run for reelection in a "breaking point" with the president on his sweeping tax and spending cuts package, is publishing the book in his final months in office. He joins a long list of Republicans who have ratcheted up their public denunciations of Trump once they had less to lose politically. Still, Tillis mostly deflects full blame from Trump, saying, "my beef is not with him, but the idiots he's got working for him." He calls the president "an amazing political talent." At the same time, he warns of a slippery slope toward authoritarianism and urges his colleagues to "wake up" and push back on Trump more often, for their own political good. Executive overreach, he says, doesn't work and sooner or later, "comes back to bite the majority party in the ass." Tillis also predicts a "bloodbath" for Republicans in November's midterm elections. "All along, we've had multiple chances to get off the path and avoid the giant bronze monster chasing us down," he writes. Regrets his votes for Hegseth and Kennedy The book is filled with cuss words and condemnations. He criticizes Trump's tariffs, the aggressive immigration raids that Tillis says were an effort to "intentionally sow disorder" and the Iran war, which he initially supported. He said the war can only end with a coalition of willing nations and if Trump gets "Pete Hegseth the hell out of the way." Tillis pushed Hegseth's confirmation vote late into the evening on Jan. 24, 2025, as he weighed his decision, talking to the White House, people who had worked with Hegseth and Hegseth himself. In the end, he said he couldn't corroborate the worst allegations and would support Hegseth's confirmation. His vote brought the total to 50-50, and Vice President JD Vance broke the tie. On his vote for Kennedy, Tillis writes that "I guess it's easy to say now, but I'm the one who has to live with that vote and all the havoc Kennedy's tenure has caused the country as a result." On both votes, he says he didn't want to be the deciding factor. "I had no intention of letting my colleagues outsource their courage to me while they pretended to go along with the questionable nomination President Trump had put forward," he writes. If you oppose Trump on everything, "you lose all influence," Tillis says. "If you oppose him and lose, you are in even worse shape." He strongly criticizes several of Trump's other initial picks for the Cabinet in the book, including former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Tillis describes his 'breaking point' over the tax bill Tillis's surprise announcement in June 2025 that he wouldn't be running for reelection came as he escalated criticism against Trump and his "Big Beautiful Bill" of tax and spending cuts. Trump attacked Tillis on social media after the senator said he couldn't support the bill's cuts to Medicaid. Tillis says he thought to himself, "I'm done." "Everyone reaches a breaking point," he writes. He texted the president asking him to look for his replacement in the Senate, to which Trump replied "I am! DJT." In May 2026, Trump again attacked Tillis, calling him a "QUITTER!" on social media, among other insults. Tillis ends the book with a profanity-laced text he sent to the president in response. "I care if you fail and right now we are failing," Tillis wrote to Trump. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez's decision to call a snap election for 29 November came on the back of a parliamentary defeat.
On Friday, the raft of measures he had presented to congress aimed at improving conditions for tenants and trying to address the problem of soaring rentals was narrowly rejected, as parties on the right voted against them.
That parliamentary result confirmed that SÃ¡nchez's left-wing coalition no longer commanded a majority.
But as has so often been the case throughout SÃ¡nchez's career, the calling of the election was not a knee-jerk reaction but a carefully thought-out manouevre.
His government has been struggling in recent months.
His Socialist Party has been mired in corruption, with cases implicating former senior figures in the party, Santos CerdÃ¡n and JosÃ© Luis Ãbalos, while the former Socialist Prime Minister, JosÃ© Luis RodrÃguez Zapatero, is facing accusations of having benefited financially from the government's bailout of an airline. Zapatero has denied wrongdoing.
In addition, SÃ¡nchez's wife, BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez, is due to go on trial over allegations of misuse of funds and influence peddling - accusations that GÃ³mez and SÃ¡nchez vehemently deny.
Meanwhile, SÃ¡nchez's administration has struggled to manage the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa, where more than 70,000 migrants suddenly arrived in July. Most have returned over the border to Morocco, but the city has become a political and logistical headache for the prime minister.
Although SÃ¡nchez had insisted until recently that he would see out the legislature and not call elections until next summer, his government had looked increasingly unlikely to make it that far.
The wave of outrage which has exploded in recent days over housing has provided him with the ideal reason to call elections early - and a welcome issue away from Ceuta and the allegations of corruption.
Appealing to his own party's voters and those further to the left on Monday, he called for voters to "mobilise and ensure that parliament gives us a much bigger, progressive majority with which to defeat the elites, conquer social rights and keep transforming Spain".
On the upcoming campaign trail, SÃ¡nchez can point to the fact that his adversaries on the right - such as the conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox - voted against his government's housing measures, which sought to prevent the eviction of tenants, improving the conditions of their contracts and preventing investors from buying residential property.
The PP and Vox tend to oppose any initiative presented by the SÃ¡nchez government, which they have long cast as illegitimate due to its scandals and reliance on Catalan and Basque nationalists.
However, as a matter of policy, parties on the right tend to oppose the kind of direct intervention in the housing market that SÃ¡nchez has been advocating, warning that it can be counterproductive.
Earlier this year, when SÃ¡nchez's international profile rose due to his outspoken criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza and his clashes with US President Donald Trump, there was speculation that he might have used the political capital that gave him on the left and called an early election back then.
However, the housing issue, which is the biggest concern for Spaniards according to polls, appears more likely to mobilise support on the left.
Yet polls also show that the Socialists are trailing the PP. While the housing issue provides SÃ¡nchez with a potential fillip on the campaign trail, staying in power after these elections will be probably the biggest challenge of his career.

The News
Reflection AI, the startup billing itself as Americaâs answer to open-source Chinese AI, is releasing its first model, called Beam.
The company, founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers, is positioning Beam as a âworkhorseâ that performs better than other Western open models. The model is particularly strong at coding and agentic tasks, cofounder and CEO Misha Laskin told Semafor. It also needs three to four times less computing power to reason through a problem than comparable open models, he said, making it faster and cheaper to run.
The modelâs capabilities are comparable to one of Chinaâs Z.aiâs recent models, GLM-5.2, which was released in June; Beam is âapproachingâ the performance of Alibabaâs most advanced model, Qwen 3.8-Max, which trails the top closed American models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
Chinaâs startups and tech giants have led the world in open-source AI. Several large Western companies have recently embraced Chinese models as a way to reduce costs for certain repetitive tasks like customer service and writing routine code. Beijing has also promoted open source as a diplomatic tool to help other countries in their tech development. But because open models can be downloaded and run with fewer safeguards, their rise has also raised security concerns: US and UK government evaluators found that recent Chinese models could help hackers exploit code vulnerabilities.
New York-based Reflection sees a large market in businesses, governments, and other entities building sovereign AI systems that donât or canât use Chinese models, but still want to âownâ and control how they use AI, Laskin said.
âThey donât really have very good options today,â he said.
Reflection is already training its next model, which Laskin said would be âmuch moreâ powerful and performant than Beam.
Know More
The startup, which has investments from Nvidia, Sequoia, and Citigroup, in June confirmed it closed its latest funding round at a $25 billion pre-money valuation. With Beamâs release, Reflection joins a slate of other Western startups, including Thinking Machines Lab and Mistral, that also offer open-weight AI models.
Its release comes as calls for AI regulation reach a fever pitch in the US, after a slate of alarming security incidents. The leading US AI labs and tech companies signed what US President Donald Trump called a âmorally bindingâ agreement on safety principles following a White House meeting.
Trump has pushed for companies to regulate themselves, rather than subject them to federal oversight, but the political calculus could shift quickly should the Democrats take over Congress in November.
Reflection says it wants to enable âbuilders of open models to be able to contribute to the discourse that is happening in DC on regulation,â Laskin said.
âYou want multiple voices around the table, both open and closed, and they should be working collaboratively on helping the government regulate AI,â he said. âWe see this entrance as something that enables more open model perspectives to be part of the discourse in DC.â
Laskin said Reflection is working with both the US Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence and the UKâs AI Safety Institute to assess the modelâs capabilities.

It's an issue that is top of mind for voters worried that their groundwater here is being polluted by the industry's waste. Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor, is tapping into the angst as part of her appeal to conservative areas that she hopes will be part of a victory in the Republican-leaning state. "This is not a partisan issue, that we need to protect our water," she told a crowd of about two dozen gathered at a riverfront gazebo, adding that cleanup costs could be well over $1 billion. "We will all pay for this mistake. So that's why we must act now." She got some help during the recent appearance, Acton's fourth to the Appalachian county that hasn't backed Democrats in years. She was joined by Susan Vessels, a prominent local Republican who had decided to forgo her own party's nominee for governor, tech billionaire and former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. Vessels, president of the city council in Marietta, praised Acton for her willingness to listen to local residents' concerns about the risks posed by fracking. She said she and others have been frustrated in their attempts to get lawmakers to do the same. "It is a pro-drinking water position, and it should be easy for any leader to support," Vessels said. Ramaswamy has been a strong supporter of developing American energy sources, including through fracking: "Unlock American energy. Drill, frack, burn coal, embrace nuclear," he said during a 2024 presidential debate. More recently in Marietta, he said he wants an economic boom that protects Ohio's natural resources and "the water quality of our communities." Both major candidates for governor are pursuing a rural strategy Acton has been campaigning throughout Ohio, with a focus on areas that have been voting Republican, especially since President Donald Trump emerged on the political stage. It's a nod to the reality of Democrats trying to win a statewide race in Ohio, a former swing state where Republicans dominate the Legislature, hold all statewide offices and elected two Republicans for the U.S. Senate. US President Donald Trump listens as Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy speaks during a rally at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio, US, October 3, 2026. Photo by Nathan Howard/REUTERS The last time a Democrat won the governor's race in Ohio was 2006. As they vie to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, Acton and Ramaswamy are trying to appeal to voters in places like Marietta against a backdrop of dissatisfaction over rising gas, grocery and healthcare costs, the war in Iran and AI data centers. Surveys show rural Americans are deeply distressed about the state of the economy. Acton, the state's health director during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, marched in Marietta's Fourth of July parade marking the nation's 250th anniversary. Ramaswamy, who has been endorsed by Trump, hosted a veterans' town hall there on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terror attacks. "Voters are frustrated, and it's not just with one political party," Ramaswamy campaign manager Jonathan Ewing said. "They're frustrated by an insider system that they see as working for one connected class of people and not for them." He said Ramaswamy is from outside that system and "can't be bought." Ramaswamy, who has landed endorsements from farming groups and the National Rifle Association, also made a stop at Schafer Leather, a thriving downtown business where customers can buy cowboy boots, wallets, belts or a Gun Tote'n Mama handbag. Staff members say they're fully in the GOP nominee's corner, despite concerns over the soaring price of gas since Trump launched the Iran war. Sherry Bailey, the store's 62-year-old sales clerk, said her core values align best with the GOP. "I believe in the Lord and the family and being free Americans," she said. Democrats target voters who believe they're being ignored That sort of party loyalty has only seemed to grow in Ohio during the Trump era, as he has won increasing shares of the vote in counties such as Washington, where he got 71% support in 2024. But Ohio Democrats aren't letting that discourage them. They say rural areas where residents are now represented by Republican majorities from their county commissions to the statehouse to Congress are growing weary of one-party rule. A statewide listening tour involving hundreds of voters across parties last year led Democrats to believe that people in three distinct groups can be persuaded, said Chris Gibbs, chair of the Ohio Democrats Rural Caucus. They identified disaffected Democrats, engaged but undecided independents and legacy Republicans, who he defined as those "disgusted with how they've seen their party go into the MAGAsphere." Democrats say new tariffs imposed under Trump, war-related increases in gas and fertilizer prices and Medicaid cuts to rural hospitals have particularly upset rural voters. Among the converts is independent Scott Oancea. As he awaited his turn at the pool table at Marietta Moose Lodge 1823 on a recent afternoon, the 64-year-old retired graphic designer said he voted once for Trump but will be supporting Democrats up and down the ticket this year. "I would vote as much as I can against Trump, to neutralize him," he said. "I'm shocked by what's happening. It's an insane situation. He wants to tear down buildings that have been there for 50

Pentagon, FBI personnel-data breaches raise questions
The defense breach, which exposed about 3 million people, went undetected for months.
A Pentagon breach that exposed sensitive personnel information for months is raising questions yet again about federal agencies' ability to detect unauthorized access to their records.
Information about roughly 3 million people was potentially exposed from October 2025 to July 16, 2026, by a breach of a file-sharing system at the Defense Manpower Data Center, which maintains personnel information used across the military and other government agencies.
“Three million people may be the headline, but months of unauthorized access to highly sensitive data going undetected is the real warning,” said Nitay Milner, co-founder and CEO of data security company ORION Security.
Nextgov/FCW obtained a copy of the letter, which was signed by DMDC Director Katie Griffin. The accessed files contained unencrypted personal information, including Social Security numbers and, depending on the individual, names, birth dates, contact information and military occupational specialties.
“Upon discovery of the security vulnerability, DMDC immediately initiated privacy and cybersecurity incident response actions in accordance with Office of the Management and Budget and [Defense] Department guidelines and policies,” Griffin wrote. “We are taking appropriate actions to assess and enhance the cybersecurity posture of the DMDC system.”
DMDC patched the flaw and restored the system, according to the letter, and affected individuals are being offered a year of credit monitoring and identity-restoration services.
Military Times first reported the incident late last month, citing the same notice. A defense official later told CNN that the breach affected 2.76 million living people and another 294,000 deceased individuals.
The disclosure comes as the FBI responds to a separate breach claimed by prolific cybercrime group ShinyHunters, which likely exposed sensitive records of personnel involved in intelligence-gathering roles.
No public evidence has linked the intrusions, though both cases involve information that could help attackers identify government personnel and tailor attempts to deceive them through fraud schemes. Such data can also identify employees whose work is of particular interest to foreign intelligence services.
The breach is hardly the first to expose weaknesses in federal systems in recent years. In December 2024, Treasury disclosed that Chinese state-sponsored hackers accessed unclassified documents through a compromised remote-support service. Separately, the federal judiciary acknowledged attacks on its electronic case management system in August 2025, and the Congressional Budget Office confirmed unauthorized access to its systems that November.
AI systems are widely expected to accelerate cyberattacks, helping hackers find security weaknesses and use stolen personal information to make their targeting more precise and convincing.
Milner said detecting unauthorized activity requires agencies to understand who is gathering sensitive information, whether they are permitted to enter a given system and whether their behavior makes sense.
That scrutiny can matter even when an intrusion doesn’t immediately disrupt a system or draw attention. In the case of DMDC, the department’s notification described access spanning roughly nine months before the vulnerability was discovered.
Jeff Wichman, senior director of breach preparedness and response at Semperis, said agencies must plan for intrusions even when they have experienced security teams and established protections.
“The FBI and Pentagon have amazing responders, but these breaches are still happening and eventually everyone is hit,” he said. “True resilience depends on having a fully pressure-tested incident response plan detailing exactly which teams are responsible for what across the entire breach cycle, from initial discovery and containment to legal and regulatory reporting.”
He also warned that new government AI services, including the America.gov chatbot, could create more ways for attackers to reach sensitive information if those tools connect to agency systems. “More government agencies will fall victim to compromise,” he said. “Every piece of leaked data creates a domino effect.”

d42622ddd5e5.text: By — Maria Ramirez Uribe Maria Ramirez Uribe Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/what-to-know-about-a-russian-lab-workers-death-and-speculation-about-pneumonic-plague Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about a Russian lab worker's death and speculation about pneumonic plague World Oct 5, 2026 6:25 PM EDT Local officials have confirmed the illness and death of a lab worker at an anti-plague research institute in Russia. A lack of transparency about the events and conflicting reports about the type of illness and how the young woman was infected have fueled concerns and speculations about a suspected case of pneumonic plague. In a statement to state media, the country's health and consumer protection agency, Rospotrebnadzor, said the employee was diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology." However, a local official previously described the woman as having died "possibly from plague." Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. was aware of the incident and "monitoring it closely." "I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus," Rubio told reporters Monday. Here's what we know and don't know so far. What are official sources saying? Official accounts have varied. The woman's name and age have not been confirmed. But officials say she worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and Far East, which focuses on plague control and works with dangerous bacterial and viral infections, according to its website. The research body is located in the city of Irkutsk, about 3,000 miles east of Russia's capital, Moscow, and north of Mongolia. Maxim Modin, the mayor of Shelekhovsky, a district of Irkutsk Oblast, confirmed a quarantine was in place at the Shelekhovsky District Hospital, in Telegram posts on Oct. 1 and 2, after saying he received many messages from residents asking for updates. He said the hospital had suspended discharges and admissions and laboratory operations, but the outpatient clinic was still operating. He did not mention the lab worker's death or illness. A local outlet reported the lab worker had died at the Shelekhovsky hospital. READ MORE: A Russian report says a worker at a Siberian plague research institute fell ill and died of an unknown cause On Oct. 2, Igor Kobzev, governor of the Irkutsk Oblast region, confirmed via a Telegram post that he was hosting an "extraordinary meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission" with the head of Rospotrebnadzor. The country's chief sanitary doctor, Anna Yuryevna Popova, was in attendance. Kobzev said the meeting occurred after information emerged "about a suspected case of a regional resident with a particularly dangerous infection." He described the situation as "under strict control," and said the consumer protection agency had implemented "a full range of anti-epidemic measures." That same day, Alexey Tsydenov, the head of the neighboring Republic of Buryatia, described the woman's death as being caused by the "plague," as he was responding to reports that she had previously traveled to the region. News outlets say Tsydenov later edited the post adding the word "possibly." "There are no plague outbreaks in the republic, including in the area bordering Mongolia," he said. "The source of the infection is circumstances unrelated to Buryatia." On Oct. 4, Rospotrebnadzor told state news agency TASS that it was responding to a case involving a lab employee "who was diagnosed with pneumonia of unknown etiology." The agency did not mention the woman's death. On Monday, Kobzev echoed the consumer protection agency's wording, but described it as the woman's cause of death. He clarified that "microorganisms associated with her professional activities were not detected in the patient's samples," and that no employees from the institute had sought medical attention in the past several days. Local officials warned people not to visit the town of Shelekhov in a Telegram post that they later deleted, according to independent local news outlet People of Baikal. What have local and independent media outlets said? People of Baikal identified the worker as a 28-year-old lab technician and said she died of the pneumonic plague. The news outlet cited local journalist Pavel Stepanov, who reported the lab worker was infected after she broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague bacterium. It also reported that a state television channel deleted five articles it had published about the incident. Rospotrebnadzor said in a statement to TASS that the institute had identified "no emergency situations involving pathogenic microorganisms." Health authorities hospitalized 189 people who had been in contact with the lab worker, according to The Moscow Times, an independent Russian news outlet. Local news outlet IrCity reported that a city cleanup event had been canceled as part of safety measures being taken "due to the unfavorable epidemiological situation." What is the pneumonic plague? Plague is a severe and often fatal disease caused by a bacteria known as Yersinia pestis, which is often found in small mammals and fleas, according to the World Health Organization. People are infected through bites from infected fleas, contact with infected tissues or inhalation of infected respiratory particles. There are three main kinds of plague: bubonic, pneumonic and septicaemic. Bubonic plague is the likely cause of the Black Death, the pandemic that hit Europe in the mid-1300s. READ MORE: The U.S. sees 7 plague cases a year. Here's why Pneumonic plague is a respiratory disease characterized by rapidly developing pneumonia, shortness of breath, chest pain and cough, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
