Belgian physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space, shedding light on the distant universe.
Halzen led the development of IceCube at the South Pole, which uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice fitted with light sensors to detect particles called neutrinos. These carry information about violent, high-energy processes in the cosmos.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said "his vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory".
Halzen first presented his vision for detecting neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988.
"Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument," said Mark Pearce, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics.
"His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy,"
Neutrinos are elusive subatomic particles. The Sun produces vast numbers of them: every second, billions pass harmlessly through an area the size of your fingernail.
But IceCube is searching for much higher-energy neutrinos, those produced by violent processes far beyond our Solar System â in distant galaxies.
Neutrinos can be thought of as astronomical messengers that point to those fundamental events.
At the observatory, most neutrinos pass straight through the ice, but occasionally one interacts with it, producing particles that give off a telltale flash of light.
These rare signals carry clues to where the neutrinos came from and the extreme conditions that produced them â allowing scientists to investigate places that ordinary telescopes cannot easily see.

5f308b642388.text: President Trump has long nicknamed his opponents, and now, as November approaches, he's even trying to dictate the vocabulary around key issues . The big picture: Trump's latest effort to reshape political language follows his longtime political strategy: Define the terms of the debate, and you gain power over the debate itself. But as polling on those issues continues to haunt the president's party, Trump's new vocabulary may not be enough to change voters' minds. Case in point: Americans are worried about AI — but to Trump, that word no longer exists. It's "super intelligence" now. Voters are also concerned about affordability, but that's a "new word" and a "hoax," Trump says. And the war in Iran? Sometimes Trump says it's a war — a word that carries strict legal implications — and other times it's an "excursion," a "military operation" or a "skirmish." The intrigue: The issues are starkly different, but the throughline is the way Trump frames the linguistic building blocks of political debate. "If you can actually get everyone who influences our perception of language to adopt your language, you have a very powerful capacity," says Kathleen Hall Jamieson, a communications professor at the University of Pennsylvania and director emerita of the Annenberg Public Policy Center. What they're saying: "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement to Axios. The latest: As fears about AI's potential threat to humanity (which the president has labeled a "hoax") boiled over, Trump — who has favored a light regulatory touch — signed an executive order replacing "artificial" with a different word: "super." "This is a highly contentious issue right now that is working against him because his position is unpopular ," Jamieson says. She adds: "But AI … is so pervasive right now in the news environment and the anxieties of the culture that if you can attach positive affect to it as opposed to negative affect to it, you've accomplished something." The reaction has been mixed: Elon Musk said he'd rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, but Sam Altman told Politico he wouldn't rename OpenAI, noting that "brands are sticky." Zoom in: Trump is also fighting an uphill battle against the word "affordability": a simple term for complex economic strain that Democrats harnessed in key elections and have championed throughout the midterm cycle. He's said it's a word the press devised, a " fake word " and a Democratic " con job ." But unlike with SI, he hasn't offered an alternative. But he's also leaned on his own midterm buzz words, "communism" being a prime example . Between the lines: " If you can shape which words are used in a political debate and how those words are defined, then you've won the debate before it even starts," explains Jennifer Mercieca, a Texas A&M professor and author of "Demagogue for President: The Rhetorical Genius of Donald Trump." "President Trump knows this, of course, and has been very successful in re-framing or re-defining issues," she writes to Axios, pointing to his popularization of the term "fake news." But Trump's "frame warfare isn't surprising" as "it is essential to how politics works today." Trump's second administration has expanded that battle over language, renaming the Gulf of Mexico , Lake Ontario and the Department of Defense . Keywords tied to diversity and gender have driven grant cancellations. And with Trump's punitive response to anyone who doesn't use his preferred language, Jamieson says: "You may be adding a function to the presidency, a controversial function, which is namer-in-chief." The bottom line: Our perceptions can be shaped by language — but the key question for November is whether our elections can be. Go deeper: Inside Trump's "super intelligence" naming problem

10f0aa8e71af.text:
Andyâs view
For at least a quarter of a century, US military strategists have calculated that if China moved aggressively against Washingtonâs allies in Asia â by imposing a naval blockade on Taiwan, or threatening Japanâs vital sea lanes â the US Navy could, as a last resort, weaponize oil against Beijing.
Most of Chinaâs seaborne oil imports flow through the Strait of Malacca, a narrow waterway that links the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. Block that passage, the thinking went, and Chinaâs economy would be crippled.
The war in Iran has shattered those assumptions. Not only has Chinaâs economy survived the oil supply disruption largely unscathed, but its enormous oil stockpiles, overland pipelines, new technologies to convert coal to chemicals, and embrace of green technologies have given Beijing strategic leverage. By contrast, the island economies around China, including Japan, Taiwan, and the Philippines â all overwhelmingly reliant on imported energy â are struggling.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, is facing the increasingly fraught economic and political fallout of rising inflation as a result of the energy shock.
As long ago as 2003, former Chinese leader Hu Jintao raised concerns about what he called the âMalacca Dilemma,â revealing a deep insecurity that has been a key driver of Beijingâs industrial, military, and diplomatic strategy ever since. Indeed, the trillion-dollar Belt & Road Initiative is in large part a defensive maneuver, born of a desire to reduce Chinaâs susceptibility to maritime threats from the US by looking inland to the vast Eurasia continent.
Today, Beijing has transformed what was once a chronic vulnerability into a source of strength and begun to redraw the geopolitical map of its region.
Eyck Freymann, a Hoover fellow at Stanford University and the author of Defending Taiwan, believes that now, a US blockade would have the opposite effect. âYouâd starve out your allies before you starve out China,â he told me.
Itâs no coincidence, Freymann said, that China has intensified its âgrey zoneâ intimidation of smaller neighbors over the past several months as war in Iran drags on, prolonging the energy crisis.
Chinese coast guard vessels have increased patrols off Taiwanâs east coast, part of a wider campaign to assert law enforcement control over shipping routes around the island. Those moves have alarmed Japan, whose economy is dependent for its survival on open sea lines and which recently has been embroiled in a spat with China over remarks that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made about Taiwan. Beijing has also been stepping up its territorial claims within Philippine waters.
The blunt message that Beijing is sending, said Freymann, is that now, âChinaâs boss.â
Whatâs more, noted James Crabtree, the author of the forthcoming The Perimeter â on the âFirst Island Chainâ in the western Pacific that he describes as the worldâs most important geopolitical fault line â the Iran war has further exposed the vulnerability of US bases in the Asia Pacific, all within easy reach of Chinese missiles, while putting pressure on the US aircraft carrier force. For the first time in decades, the US 7th Fleet has no carriers operating in the Indo-Pacific.
With China emerging from the Iran conflict âlooking relatively good,â said Crabtree, âthe US now has decisions to makeâ on its military deployments in the region.
Some analysts argued that in striking Iran the US was actually delivering a devastating blow to China, its main geopolitical adversary and the primary customer of Iranian oil. Zineb Riboua, a researcher at the Hudson Institute, wrote that âthe road to the Pacific runs through Tehran.â
In reality, China has demonstrated it has built multiple routes to escape an energy blockade; in effect, it has resolved its âMalacca Dilemmaâ â and turned the tables on Washington. US allies now face their own existential predicament, just as war in Iran depletes American power in the region.
Notable
- The former Indian ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Oman, and the UAE writes that âthe likelihood of Malacca being monetized and, if necessary, weaponized, appears to be growing,â which has led to innovations that aim to bypass the strait entirely, most notably the construction of a new land bridge in Thailand.

- Published
Police in Delhi detained several opposition lawmakers as they tried to march demanding the chief election commissioner resign over a controversial voter roll revision.
Main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka and other MPs were forced into a police bus. Released shortly after, they resumed their march and began a sit-in near Election Commission headquarters.
It is the latest escalation in a growing row over a nationwide revision of voter rolls.
Opposition parties accuse Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of overseeing a process that could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), an allegation both the BJP and Election Commission have rejected.
"Some of the MPs tried to take some other roads to the Election Commission building. We have officers stationed at multiple points, from where the protesters were picked up in buses and taken to different police stations," Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police Manjeet Sheoran told the BBC. The police did not disclose how many lawmakers had been detained. The opposition said 237 MPs from a range of parties participated in the march.
Tuesday's protest came just four days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a Gen Z-backed online satirical movement, organised demonstrations in Mumbai and Delhi, also demanding the CEC's resignation. The group has described those demonstrations as the beginning of a nationwide campaign and has called for another round of protests on 10 October.
At the centre of the controversy is the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
The exercise began in the eastern state of Bihar in June 2025 before being expanded to other parts of the country. The Election Commission says the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters from electoral rolls. More than 130 million names have so far been removed from draft voter lists nationwide.
Opposition parties and activists allege that many eligible voters have been wrongly excluded and accuse the poll body of conducting the process improperly.
The campaign against Kumar gathered momentum after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper reported that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over a 10-month period to decisions and orders they said had been issued in the Election Commission's name without their knowledge.
According to the report, the objections related to issues including additions and deletions from voter rolls, access to the voter database and the security of electoral data. Some concerns were linked directly to the electoral roll revision programme.
The Election Commission, a three-member body comprising the chief election commissioner and two election commissioners, defended its decision-making process, saying differing views were part of institutional functioning and that decisions had ultimately been taken unanimously.
The revelations nevertheless triggered a political backlash, with opposition leaders intensifying calls for Kumar's resignation.
Security was tightened around the Election Commission headquarters on Tuesday, with police barricading roads along the route between parliament and the commission's office.
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge described three demands as "non-negotiable": Kumar's resignation, cancellation of the SIR exercise and a return to paper ballot voting.
Mocking the election chief, Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India's lower house of parliament, tweeted: "Gyanesh, it's done, bro. Time to resign."
The BJP condemned the protests.
BJP MP Sambit Patra described them as a "sponsored attempt" to bring about a change of power through "anarchy". He accused opposition parties of seeking to undermine constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission.
The controversy has also reached India's Supreme Court, which has asked both the federal government and the Election Commission to respond to a petition alleging that Kumar took key decisions without the approval of the two other election commissioners.
The petition argues that Kumar exercised powers that belong to the commission collectively and seeks a ruling that any such actions were unauthorised.
The court indicated that Election Commission decisions must be taken either unanimously or by majority vote and suggested that decisions could be set aside if found to have bypassed that process. However, it declined to suspend Kumar at this stage, saying it would first hear the Election Commission's response and examine relevant records.
The BBC has contacted the Election Commission for comment on Tuesday's protest.

Ukraine's railways have kept the country running since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. But attacks are intensifying, with more than half of all strikes on locomotives since then occurring this year alone, according to the state-owned operator.
Yuliia Ponomarenko, 27, a marketing specialist from Kharkiv, found her journey to Warsaw last month suddenly interrupted just short of the Ukraine-Poland frontier.
"The border guards started running around and shouting "Run! Get out of the carriages! There's shelling!"
A Russian drone had just hit a locomotive near the same border, and a special train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European dignitaries, had passed through minutes before.
Passengers on Yuliia's train were kept waiting for six hours while the fire up ahead was put out and the line cleared, she says: "We were really lucky that we were delayed a little and it wasn't our train."
She is among an increasing number of Ukrainian passengers facing disruption and long delays, as air raid alerts trigger emergency evacuations far from the battlegrounds of the east.
In September alone, 5,831 trains had to be evacuated due to Russian drone attacks, state owned railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia told AFP news agency on Monday. This meant on average each day, 205 trains were stopped.
It appears to be part of a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure, with two bridges attacked in Kyiv in the past few days and passengers of a metro train caught up in one of the strikes.
Seventeen-year-old Anastasiia Ryvbalchenko has also experienced a narrow escape.
She and her fellow passengers were forced to leave their train at 4am, towards the end of a long of a journey from Odesa to Kirovohrad on 16 September.
"On my way to Odesa, there had been a lot of evacuations and now on my way back it was happening again," she says. "I was already thinking that if there was another evacuation, I just couldn't take it any more."
An hour and a half later, as passengers waited in the dark, a drone struck nearby.
"There was an extremely loud explosion and everyone started running into the woods," she said.
It is not clear what the target was, and in this case the train was not damaged, but with further explosions lighting up the night sky, Anastasiia decided not to linger, continuing her journey on foot before being picked up by her parents.
"I'm not going to travel by train anymore," she says.
Anastassia's journey was more dramatic than most, but delays â some brief, others that last for hours â are now commonplace.
Since Russian drones first started attacking moving passenger trains towards the end of 2025, the routine for passengers has become increasingly familiar: leave the train, scroll Telegram channels for updates on drone and missile launches, send messages to warn friends and family that the train is delayed.
For a railway company proud of its record for punctuality, this year's disrupted schedule is posing a major challenge.
"We used to say that that during times of war we performed better than some railways in Europe in regular times,"the head of rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, told us.
"But now the life of our passengers and crew members is the utmost priority."
Russia's defence ministry denies targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.
The dangers are very real. Attacks on Ukrzaliznytsia's rolling stock and stations have risen sharply.
Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, almost 60% have been this year, according to statistics released by the company. Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
"The latest wave of escalation and real war with railways is becoming extremely intense," said Pertsovskyi.
"It's a combination of the deadly force of their shahed drones and precision that they achieve with cameras and mesh networks so they can hit moving targets."
According to Pertsovskyi, some of Russia's most recent drones are equipped with AI tools and image recognition. Ukraine is understandably cagey about how it goes about confronting this increasingly sophisticated threat, but electronic methods to disrupt the drones' connectivity are high on the list.
"Unfortunately, this is always a cat-and-mouse game," he said.
We were given rare access to an underground bunker in Kyiv, dubbed â appropriately enough â the "Iron Command Centre", where railway staff monitor threats in real time.
On one huge video screen, colour-coded passenger and freight trains could be seen making their way along the arteries of Ukraine's vast railway network.
We watched as a red icon representing a drone appeared to loiter over Kyiv, practically above our heads at one point.
Each drone had a 100km (62-mile) circle around it. Any passenger trains inside the circle would already have been evacuated, with customers not allowed to reboard until the train was outside the circle and the drone was still moving away.
"Our mission is not to let our train or our crew members be in that immediate attack area," Pertsovskyi said.
The company's precautions appear to have kept casualties low. Its figures for 2026 show that eight company employees have been killed, six of them when a ballistic missile struck a locomotive depot in Kyiv.
During our visit to Iron Command, another air raid siren sounded in Kyiv. The city's main railway station, we were told, was being evacuated.
On a later visit to the busy station, we found passengers waiting outside the main entrance or sheltering in underground passageways. Over the tannoy came news of steady stream of delays.
Everyone knows the coming months could be among the most difficult yet.
With winter not far off, Ukrzaliznytsia is already figuring out how to deal with evacuations when the outside temperature can reach -20C or below and snow is lying heavy on the g

The News
When immigration enforcement deaths sparked bipartisan calls for Kristi Noemâs resignation, Sen. Susan Collins privately lobbied her to stop the surge in Maine. When the Commerce Department cut off sea grants for Maineâs flagship university, Collins called Secretary Howard Lutnick to save them.
And when President Donald Trump hit Canada with new tariffs, Collins negotiated on the side with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to exempt concrete and road salt â the latter a critical commodity during Maineâs long winters.
In other battleground Senate races this fall, voters must choose between a combative Democrat and a Trump-friendly Republican. Maineâs battle pits that type of Democrat, former statehouse leader Troy Jackson, against a rarer breed in Collins: Sheâs the only incumbent Senate Republican who criticizes Trump in public while using her personal connections to reverse some of his actions.
Itâs not clear whether Collinsâ backchanneling will be enough to satisfy anti-Trump voters in Maine â or at least enough of them to put her over the top yet again. But her strategy will become a national political story on Tuesday night, when Jackson and Collins kick off a series of Senate debates.
Collins told Semafor ahead of the October campaign season that her âchallenge is making sure that Mainers know what Iâve doneâ in unwinding some of the Trump administrationâs decisions. She said Maine would lose her direct line to the Trump Cabinet if Jackson wins â and thus get robbed of tangible victories.
âWhen you take that kind of adversarial approach, youâre unlikely to get the results, and I got results,â Collins said in an interview, referring to her quiet talks with Noem. âThe Troy Jackson approach would be to rant and rave about it, but never contact [her] directly.â
Despite Collinsâ frequent breaks from his administration, Trump has largely laid off her and âby and large has given her a pass and even been complimentary of her,â said Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D.
Yet he hasnât made it easy for her to repeat her past odds-defying wins in a blue state: In recent weeks heâs sought to take over National Institute of Health grants and rescinded congressionally approved spending while repeatedly antagonizing Canada, which shares hundreds of miles of border with Maine.
âHeâs making the lives of Maine families difficult, and Maineâs businesses and Maineâs communities difficult. And obviously, heâs not thinking about the implications for them or for me,â Collins said. âIâm not a focus for the president. I think thatâs probably fair to say. But working families and small businesses and communities ought to be.â
Asked to respond to Collinsâ comment, a White House official touted Trumpâs âcountless winsâ in Maine, including a reduction in homicides and his tax cut law â which Collins opposed.
Know More
Collins handily won her race in 2020 despite trailing in the polls for months to Democrat Sara Gideon. Six years later, the Maine electorate is worn out by Trump, but polls still show the race as a tossup. Collins benefited from Democratic discord as the party jettisoned its original nominee Graham Platner over sexual assault allegations, replacing him with Jackson.
The national Democratic effort to defeat Collins kept going; now the party is spending millions on an ad hitting her for a ProPublica story about her links to a corrupt defense contractor. The ad alleges that, after an FBI investigation into the matter was dropped, that âmaybe thereâs a reason Susan Collins does whatever Donald Trump wants her to.â
The typically genteel Collins has a volcanic response to that line of attack.
âAnyone who knows me or has worked with me knows that I am a person of integrity, and thatâs why Iâm so offended,â she said. âIt is clearly an attempt to try to persuade the people of Maine that Iâm not who I am.â
And even with the ProPublica report, Democrats are focused on turning the race into a referendum on Trump â and, by extension, Collinsâ complicated relationship with his administration.
âItâs hard to push back against Trump when you vote with him 96 percent of the time,â Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told Semafor. âShe has backed Trump and refused to go against so many of the bad things heâs done.â
Collins argues that her approach is consistent: Sheâs supported major nominees of presidents in both parties, opposed some moves made by both parties, and never aligned neatly with the GOP agenda. That assessment used to apply to quite a few senators in both parties. Now itâs a strange place for a Republican to be.

New technology has been installed to track how much carbon is being taken out of the atmosphere by Scotland's largest saltmarsh.
The flux tower has been put in place at Caerlaverock on the Solway Firth.
About 85% of UK saltmarshes have been lost since the mid-19th Century as land has been reclaimed from the sea for agriculture, development or coastal flood defences, degraded through pollution or eroded by rising sea levels.
Corallie Hunt, coastal habitats adviser for NatureScot, said the installation of the first saltmarsh flux tower in Scotland marked an "important milestone".
The project is a partnership between UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology (UKCEH), the Scottish government, NatureScot, and WWF-UK.
"By measuring carbon exchange in real time, it will strengthen our understanding of the carbon storage potential of saltmarshes and the value of protecting and restoring these habitats," said Hunt.
UKCEH wetland scientist Annette Burden said the Solway flux tower was the most northerly addition to a network around the UK coast.
"The data collected will aid in understanding the role saltmarsh plays in climate mitigation, provide evidence for saltmarsh inclusion in the UK Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Inventory, which in turn will strengthen calls to safeguard and restore this valuable habitat," she said.
In addition to supporting biodiversity and providing natural flood protection, the plants covering the marshes draw down carbon dioxide through photosynthesis and can also trap carbon-rich sediments in their roots and stems on the incoming tide.
Tom Brook, ocean conservation specialist at WWF said: "The Solway is an extraordinary place for nature.
"From thousands of migratory birds that depend on these wetlands to the rare natterjack toad, the saltmarsh supports an incredible variety of wildlife.
"It's also working hard for people too â helping to absorb wave energy and reduce the impacts of flooding and storm surges.
"The data gathered by the tower will help us better understand and champion the value of these remarkable coastal habitats."

88ddd3d0aa80.text: Two big unknowns stand in the way of determining how serious the plague threat in Russia is and whether travel advisories, restrictions at U.S. ports of entry or other precautions are warranted. We still don't know which pathogen killed a Russian researcher, or how well contained it is. Why it matters: Though public health experts say there's no cause for Americans to panic, the episode serves as a wake-up call emphasizing the nature of global biological threats and the need for pandemic preparedness. State of play: A worker at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East recently died after contracting pneumonia. There are conflicting accounts of how she got sick and whether she was infected with pneumonic plague, which is almost always deadly without prompt treatment with antibiotics. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the administration is closely monitoring the situation, adding, "I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on. And we're doing that." If a response is required, "the playbook for these instances is very well defined," David Mansdoerfer, a former health official in the first Trump administration, told Axios. "Traditionally, the precautionary measures the government would take would be via a travel advisory from [the State Department]," he said, adding the U.S. already has its most serious travel warning in place for Russia due to the war with Ukraine. It would also contact U.S. citizens in the affected area with guidance, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention would follow up with a travel health notice, Mansdoerfer said. "The government would then focus on [Customs and Border Protection] ill traveler rules " that can include stopping high-risk individuals from boarding flights or flagging health officials if they land at a port of entry. At that point, "it becomes a CDC protocol-driven process," he added. The intrigue: If the Russian worker did die from pneumonic plague, experts say there's a possibility that it was a genetically altered version that behaves differently than the treatable strain. That's just speculation at this point. But the prevalence of "gain-of-function" research that enhances pathogens to study them and Russia's known development of biological weapons make it impossible to rule out. U.S. preparedness efforts will focus first on getting as much detailed information as possible because officials first need to understand what is going on to prepare for it, said Tom Inglesby, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. "It's really critical to get the diagnosis right. There are conflicting stories around it," Inglesby said, noting that while there are substantial supplies of antibiotics in government stockpiles and pharmacies, there's still the possibility the strain is resistant to them. Another key unknown is if pneumonia believed to be linked to plague has spread in the community. So far, reports suggest it's limited to the lab scientist who died while others in the community are under close monitoring. "Pneumonic plague does not normally cause large outbreaks in modern times, it happens rarely but it's very uncommon," Inglesby said. "If many people in that city do get sick, that would call into question the diagnosis, or raise concerns about something else going on." "Getting the real story, the true facts of the situation out in the open is critical to everything else that follows in the response," he added. Asked whether he's concerned, President Trump on Monday said: "Somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They're like an army ... even with great advances, the germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don't work as well anymore." Friction point: Determining whether the incident resulted from legitimate plague research as opposed to a weapons program is important, considering the still-heated debate over COVID's origins and the Russian institute's connection with the nation's biowarfare apparatus. There's no credible evidence that the deceased worker at the Russian institute was involved with research on a weaponized or engineered strain. In fact, some reports state she had recently traveled to regions along the Mongolia-Russia border, where plague naturally occurs in animals. The institute where she worked was established as part of an anti-plague network and was mainly responsible for surveillance of dangerous pathogens. But it developed vaccines and diagnostics for pathogens that were modified by the military, according to the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies . A 2024 State Department assessment concluded Russia maintains an offensive bioweapons program and absorbed the old Soviet program and evolved it. The CDC says the Soviet Union in the 1970s and 1980s manufactured large quantities of antibiotic-resistant Y. pestis [the bacteria that causes plague] to be dispersed in the air as a bioweapon and that, in light of these and recent events involving terrorist organizations, the United States and other countries must be prepared for a bioterrorism attack involving Y. pestis . Zoom out: Pneumonic plague cases are rare but not unheard of, including in the U.S. Last year, the CDC launched a pneumonic plague investigation in Arizona after a young adult male died after exposure to two ill cats. Officials identified 46 potentially exposed persons, who were given antibiotics. The bottom line: In the most optimistic scenario, Russia has responded with an abundance of caution to a one-off deadly infection that hasn't spread. But there's too much that still needs to be verified to draw any conclusions.

In a little more than a decade, Octopus Energy has grown from an outlandish idea into Britainâs largest energy provider. It now powers 12 million homes in eight countries, manages wind and solar farms from Scotland to South Korea, manufactures heat pumps, installs smart meters, leases out 50,000 electric vehicles, and supplies technology to utilities around the world.
The tentacles of this âOctoverseâ all lead back to Greg Jackson, a founder-CEO who has built his 13,000-person company without bonuses, HR or IT teams, or a succession plan.
Beyond the walls of the companyâs London headquarters, which is filled with thousands of its plushy pink octopus mascots, Jacksonâs empire may look like an unwieldy one. It is not, he insists: âThe thing thatâs connecting it all is the underlying insight: that the technologies of electrification can deliver tremendous cost savings, but only if you build a new system.â And building that new system requires using every tool at his disposal.
âThereâs a scene in the movie Apollo 13 where the astronauts are stranded and theyâre going to die unless the solution is found. And on the ground, Mission Control assembles â¦ everything there is on the space station, like duct tape and bits of piping, and they say, this is all weâve got to save their lives,â he explains. âIn any business, you choose your constraints, and then how you assemble the stuff you have to create the outcome you want.â
Octopusâ job is âto take all these ingredients and say, how can we outcompete the old world of energy with better products and services with better value?â Jackson says, before reaching back to the beginning of that old world for another analogy.
âWhen [Thomas] Edison first started building electricity businesses, he didnât just have to innovate, fund, and build centralized electricity generation, which he did. He also had to invent the grid and distribution model. He also had to invent or sell the products that use electricity, from lightbulbs to music players. And if I look at what weâre doing, itâs almost trivial in comparison.â
How to run a 13,000-person company with no HR department
The growth of Octopus, which had revenues of Â£13.7 billion last year and a valuation of $9 billion at its last fundraising, poses a challenge for its irrepressible founder: how to transmit to thousands of employees the energy that has powered him since he dropped out of school at 16 to write video games.
Jackson no longer knows each staff member by name, but he still runs his company by the same rhythms with which he started it. Each Monday starts with a gathering of senior executives to review performance data from the previous week. That helps maintain âpace and alignment,â Jackson says. Each week ends with âfamily dinner,â a Friday afternoon all-hands event at which the company recaps its latest innovations, achievements, and challenges.
The Friday sessions began over beers with a small founding team, and Jackson âdiscovered that it was the best way of reminding you how great your colleagues were, and re-energizing you on the big picture.â Livestreams have since replaced in-person drinks. But the gatherings help Octopus âstart the week left-brain, end it right-brain,â Jackson says, and help him explain to staff what they need to do next âand maintain the energy to feel great about it.â
The company has no intranet or staff newsletters, he adds, so if people donât tune in to âfamily dinner,â they wonât know whatâs happening. Less is more in internal communications, he says: âThe more information you put out there, the less it gets read. What you want to do is make sure the stuff that goes out there is canonical and consumed.â
Octopus also has no central human resources department, devolving people management responsibilities to individual teams unless legal staff need to step in. Still a private company, it gives equity to every employee, but it pays no bonuses outside a few sales roles. Jackson says this is because heâs determined to focus people on the companyâs success, rather than their own individual advancement.
Similarly, Octopus sets no divisional performance targets, to keep each division from promoting whatever will make them look best at the expense of others, he adds.
âThe most important thing for us is to build trust among our team, so they wake up every morning thinking, âHow do I drive the companyâs mission?â Not, âHow do I get myself promoted?ââ
Hands-on leadership, from the cockpit to the customers
Even as Octopus has grown to span industries as diverse as renewable power generation and software licensing, Jackson says his job has barely changed. The CEOâs role is still to understand customers and industry economics; set the vision for where the company needs to go; and build a team with the expertise and innovative impulses to get it there.
For a pilot, the view from the cockpit window of a small Cessna is not that different from that of an Airbus A380, he says: âThe difference comes when you look back.â If Octopus became a more complex organization, âthen Iâd get drawn more into wandering down the aisle of the plane than looking forward out the window,â he reasons. âThe bit that really matters for me is being in the cockpit, looking forward, however many people weâve got behind us.â So Jackson is constantly checking that his headcount is not growing faster than Octopus is adding new customers, as he looks to avoid diseconomies of scale and guards against the spread of bureaucracy. Yet he is equally anxious about ensuring that he is not losing touch with customers as their numbers run into the millions.Â
Octopus was built on a proprietary technology platform called Kraken, which it spun off as a standalone company after a fundraising that valued the former subsidiary at $8.7 billion. BlackRock is ramping up its commitments to the Gulf as the worldâs largest asset manager seeks to boost exposure to a region that it expects to use more of its vast state wealth to invest domestically in the wake of the Iran war.
Despite no resolution to the conflict, now in its eighth month and keeping the Gulf in a state of suspended uncertainty, the firm is âundiminished in our focusâ on the region, said Ben Powell, chief investment strategist for the Middle East and Asia-Pacific at the BlackRock Investment Institute.
Counterintuitively, the bullishness stems from the regionâs relative stability: âIn terms of the rules of the game, the positive attitude towards business, not to mention human capital, financial capital, energy â¦ I feel very confident that this is a story that is true and real and going to play out over the next five, 10 years,â he said.
Stability âin a world of great moderation, thatâs not that interesting,â Powell said. âBut in a world of excitement, that becomes much rarer â¦ it is worth 10 times what it was in a world where everythingâs okay.â
And increasingly, everything is not okay. Powellâs broader outlook is that persistent inflation, fragmentation, and higher capital costs will make investors more selective. âWeâre all going to be incorrect more often â¦ Where you can find confidence, grab it with both hands because itâs in short supply,â he said.
Know More
BlackRock, which manages more than $15 trillion, has offices in Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Riyadh, Doha, and Kuwait City. Powell said the Gulf will âcontinue to be a significant exporter of capital,â but that âat the margin, maybe some portion of that money that was going to flow out is going to stay at home.â He put the amount at $50 billion to $100 billion, and cautioned that the estimate has wide error bands. Powell tied that shift to the $2.1 trillion in strategic capital spending the institute estimates the Gulf states will make in its diversification push through 2030.
The bigger change, he said, is a focus on âsocietal and economic resilienceâ across energy, infrastructure, and the regionâs build-out for AI, including âsome projects where we hope utilization rates will be very low.â
Some of that spending is âalmost an insurance policy,â Powell said: âWeâre going to build pipelines we hope we never use.â
Through âa solely economic lens, that would not make much sense,â he said, but the need for redundancy as global geopolitical tensions rise means it makes âall the sense in the world.â
Powell also expects more spending where AI, energy, and defense overlap. âTheyâre all kind of the same thing now,â he said.
Step Back
BlackRockâs Global Infrastructure Partners is part of a $30 billion infrastructure partnership with Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund LâIMAD, national oil company ADNOC, and Singaporeâs Temasek, announced in May.
The asset manager is among a growing number of global firms in Abu Dhabiâs financial center, ADGM, drawn by proximity to sovereign wealth funds like ADIA and Mubadala, family offices, and the regionâs expanding appetite for private credit. Gulf capital is still flowing out at a record pace: the regionâs sovereign wealth funds invested $53.9 billion across 108 transactions in the first half of 2026, an all-time high, according to Global SWF.
Notable
- Singaporeâs Temasek will open its first offices in the Gulf early next year, joining a growing list of global investors expanding into the region despite ongoing conflict.
- OpenAI is in talks with BlackRock and UAE funds, including Abu Dhabiâs MGX, to raise as much as $30 billion, Bloomberg reported.

Leaders in California have condemned President Trump following comments he made during a midterms election rally in Nebraska.
Speaking about higher gas prices as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, Trump said Tehran "taking out" Los Angeles or San Diego would be a "small price to pay for keeping the world safe".
State governor Gavin Newsom described the US president as "deranged and dangerous," while Mayor of Los Angeles Karen Bass said: "The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives."
The cities are the largest in southern California and house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.
Trump described the war with Iran as almost over while speaking in Nebraska, and there were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.
San Diego's Mayor Todd Gloria wrote the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk".
In a second post on his official governor of California X account, Newsom shared an article on the comments from the Los Angeles Times saying it was "disgusting and disqualifying".
Trump is yet to respond to the comments made by California's leaders.
San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast.
It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at.
Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US.
It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.
This not the first time the US president and California governor, who may run for president in 2028, have publicly clashed.
Last year Trump described him as incompetent, saying he had failed to adequately respond after some of the Los Angeles anti-immigration enforcement protests turned violent.
Newsom accused Trump of a "brazen abuse of power" after military personnel were deployed to secure federal buildings during those protests.
Earlier this year, Trump mocked Newsom's dyslexia, saying presidents should not have learning disabilities, which led to criticism from dyslexia charities.

Meet Jules Rodriguez. He’s a dad, husband, former science teacher, podcaster and stand-up comedian — someone who has always had a lot to say.
But ALS has taken away his ability to speak. Now, Jules communicates by typing with his eyes, and an AI-generated voice clone speaks his words aloud.
What do we lose when we lose our voice?
In this episode of The Deep End, hear Jules’ story, as well as perspectives from scientists and clinicians on why a voice is so much more than a way to communicate. Human brains are poised to seek out voices, and all the various kinds of information they can hold.
Jules’ experience reveals just how much of our identity is created by the way we sound — and what it means when that sound disappears.
Episode 1 transcript

Sanders: He even does some of the most terrifying talking I can imagine. He performs in front of crowds as a stand-up comedian.
Jules: I have to pick my battles. Do I want to be right or do I want to eat tonight?
Sanders: His wife, Maria Aleandra Fernandez, who goes by MA, says that Jules’ voice is one of her very favorites.
MA: Oh man, I definitely love hearing Jules’ voice. I’m not just saying that, but I do.
Sanders: Jules was born and raised in Miami. He and MA have a nine-year-old son named Skyler. Jules loves baseball. He loves the Marlins. He loves being outside. He loves action.
Jules: I was always pretty high energy. I loved mountain biking, snorkeling, fishing, and playing all sports, really. Baseball is my favorite sport to play and watch.
Sanders: The night Jules and MA met, they were doing karaoke at her 30th birthday party.
MA: A friend introduced us, and it was kind of a, sort of a love at first sight situation. We danced, we sang.

MA: “Baby Got Back,” yeah. That one he got up there and sang with a couple of his friends. It was like him and his three other buddies that were there with him. And oh, that was just so joyous. And we had karaoke at our wedding as well, so, we’ve always loved to sing, to dance. We took ballroom dancing classes. We, like, danced at every wedding. All of it. So, yeah.
Sanders: You have a good time.
MA: Yeah, yeah, definitely.
Sanders: Yeah.
Sanders: One more thing about Jules. He has ALS. That’s short for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a disease also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease or motor neuron disease. Jules has lived with ALS since 2020. Many of his muscles no longer respond to his brain’s signals, which means he can’t move his body or breathe on his own. This dropped signal between brain and body also means that Jules is no longer able to talk. That line you heard earlier from Jules?
Jules: I was always pretty high energy.
Sanders: That was an AI-generated, synthetic voice speaking his words. His voice, as it used to exist, is gone.
Welcome to Season 2 of The Deep End, a podcast about our brains and ourselves. I’m your host, Laura Sanders, a reporter with Science News. And this season, called Talk to Me, is about the human voice.
[intro] Hey Mom, can I tell you something? The casual observer sees little of the vigorous activity at the site of voice production. The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.
[voice] My poor little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character. I have a dream…
Sanders: Voices can be powerful. We save and replay voicemails.
[voice] Hey, dude, I’m just calling to say hi and chit-chat.
Sanders: We call someone special just to hear their voice.
[voice] Hello. Hello.
Sanders: We love to hear people tell stories.
[voice] Mom, can you tell me a story?
Sanders: But why? What is it inside these voices that can calm us down or terrify us or have us laughing so hard we’re gasping for air? In this season, we’re going to explore a simple but deep question. What gives the human voice so much power? You’re going to hear all sorts of voices. They’ll tell a story of what connects us and what happens when those connections are lost. Over the next six episodes, we’ll explore a new digital world. In this world, human voices no longer need a human body to create them. You’ll hear how machines can speak for those who can’t, and even pull words from the brains of people who can’t speak. It’s a story about how technology is changing the human voice in ways that are good, bad, and fascinating. Let’s begin.
Sanders: People listen for voices in everything. There’s a parallel you might have heard of. It’s a weird quirk of human brains that we’re able to find faces everywhere, too. That’s why you’ve seen the shape of a face in an electrical outlet or a car grill or a random pattern on the wall. Our brains love seeing faces. And it turns out our brains love hearing voices too.
Greg Bryant: It’s really well established that there’s a voice-selective region and it’s activated really early.
Sanders: Greg Bryant is a cognitive scientist who studies vocal communications at UCLA. He tells me that there’s a spot in the brain that responds strongly to voices.
Bryant: Yeah, we hear voices in all kinds of stuff. I mean, you ever been out camping and you’re like [whispers], you know, or something, you know, you hear like whispering. And yeah, it’s really easy to hallucinate a voice.
Sanders: Part of the reason our brains tune into voices might be that they are packed with information, information that goes well beyond words.

A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say.
A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued.
Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable".
Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said.
The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania.
Tracking data shows the ship entered the Black Sea heading north on Monday. Its last reported position on MarineTraffic was at 2343 GMT last night in the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone of the Black Sea.
It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board.
A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. It was not clear how many crew members were on board. A search operation has been launched. The vessel's cargo was not immediately known.
Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain.
Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan.
Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law".
He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable."
He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict."
European Commission President von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning.
"Commercial ships â and innocent crews â are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning."
"Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable."
The government said it would convene an emergency meeting on Tuesday to discuss the strikes.
Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea.
A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media.
On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It has spread to the east of the Black Sea in recent months.
Romania reported on Monday that a grain ship had caught fire and sank in the Black Sea, with one crew member killed and one missing. Ukraine blamed the attack on Russia.

Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.
Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.
Prosecutors allege that he used classified intelligence to "draft an analysis" for one foreign intelligence service and maintained contact with another foreign spying service. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved.
Police also arrested former BND employee Mandred D, accusing him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for money.
Manfred D, who was Hanning's bureau chief and remained in the BND until this year, is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
Local media reported Hanning was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near MÃ¼nster while Manfred D was arrested in Bavaria. Hanning is due in court on Wednesday and Manfred D will appear on Tuesday.
Prosecutors say Mandred D, who also served as the chief of staff for Hanning's successors between 2012 and 2026, used his role to gain access to highly confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning "in exchange for remuneration".
"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement says.
"On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service," prosecutors said, noting it was not clear if "the material reached the intended recipient".
Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years".
Local media say Hanning's alleged possession of intelligence documents came to light during a separate case relating to German steakhouse heiress Christina Block.
Hamburg public prosecutor's office accused Block of orchestrating the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Investigators allege Hanning was involved in an earlier attempted kidnapping of the children, which he denies.
State criminal police officers reportedly discovered an electronic data storage device containing sensitive information including recent BND documents.
It is not the first time the BND has faced similar controversy. A high-ranking German intelligence officer was charged with treason in 2023 for allegedly passing state secrets to Russia.
Prosecutors alleged Carsten L shared intelligence about the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and received roughly â¬400,000 ($450,000; Â£340,000). His trial is ongoing.

Dubaiâs priciest license plate, P7, sold for $15 million in 2023. Yet the resale market has run largely on Instagram and independent brokers. A new app, Mazal, aims to change that by holding buyersâ funds in escrow until ownership is transferred, for a 5% fee. Its founders say plates worth $463 million have changed hands in three years, and that the market is growing by about 20% a year. License plates command huge sums in the Gulf, where every opportunity to signal status is welcomed â but proceeds from the government-run sales go to charity.
Mazal grades plates like gold â 18, 21, or 24 karat â with a top tier called mithali, Arabic for perfect. âThe only question is whether you are a millionaire or a billionaire,â said Chairman Abdulla AlMeer in an interview with The National. AlMeerâs green Range Rover sports a $245,000 plate. His Lamborghini, tragically, has to make do with a $136,000 one.

Saudi Arabiaâs expatriate workforce shrank for the first time in more than two years, amid layoffs, the Iran war, and a backlash against hiring foreigners at state-controlled companies. Foreigners employed in the country, excluding domestic workers, fell by 16,000 in the three months to June, driven by a drop in construction jobs, according to the governmentâs quarterly report. Medical insurance policies for expats didnât grow at all in the first six months of 2026, another indicator that fewer foreigners are coming to the kingdom.
State-controlled firms have been trimming workforces or not renewing contracts as budgets were cut for some projects, while others, like NEOM, have scaled back significantly. The Iran war has also dented the regionâs reputation for safety.
The unemployment rate for Saudi citizens hasnât budged and the economy is creating new jobs, albeit at a slower pace. Forward-looking data from the Purchasing Managersâ Index suggests hiring will bounce back.

Abu Dhabi is backing a rail link to enhance the logistics behind Jordanâs main exports. The 403-kilometer network will carry 16 million tons a year of phosphate and potash, used in fertilizers, from mines to the Port of Aqaba. The line, which will replace truck convoys and an aging freight track, is expected to cut transport costs by $40 million annually.
Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed and Jordanâs King Abdullah II broke ground on a $2.3 billion project, part of a $5.5 billion investment framework the two countries agreed to in 2023. The UAE is investing in rail infrastructure across the region, including Etihad Rail at home, Hafeet Rail to Oman, and other links that are part of a planned India-Middle East-Europe corridor, which would run through Jordan.

Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape.
The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers.
It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory.
The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network.
Paramount will acquire ownership of iconic franchises that include Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Lord of the Rings and Mission: Impossible.
The newly merged entertainment behemoth will be re-branded under the name Skydance Corporation, the company orginally founded by David Ellison before he took over both Paramount and Warner Bros Discover.
Ellison, chairman and chief executive of Skydance, said the completion of the deal was "historic" for the film industry.
"From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality," he said.
Last week, Ellison named the outgoing chief executive of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-chief executive.
Kreiz will focus on the company's day-to-day operations, including integrating the newly-combined businesses, while Ellison will focus on strategy and technology.
While the company said it had received unanimous approval from competition authorities across the world, the long running takeover process has featured controversy since the beginning.
Netflix intially had a deal to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery, but Paramount Skydance launched a bidding war, leading to the streaming giant walking away.
Lawyers in about a dozen US states then filed lawsuits - led by California - aiming to block the deal, arguing it would stifle competition, raise consumer prices and cause "substantial" harm to movie theaters, cable distributors and "ultimately, audiences nationwide".
US states announced a settlement with Paramount and Ellison last month which paved the way for the merger to go ahead.
As part of the deal, Paramount has agreed to establish a "news editorial independence board" to "ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting" at CNN and CBS.
Politics and editorial independence has become an area of concern at CBS since the news broadcaster was taken over in 2025 as part of separate a merger between Skydance Media and Paramount.
Ellison, who hosted a dinner for President Donald Trump earlier this year, has sought to reassure people that editorial independence will be maintained.
Over its 103-year-old history, Warner Bros has won more than 100 Academy Awards - including dominating at last year's show with a record-tying 11 Oscars for One Battle After Another, Sinners and Weapons.
Paramount traces its roots back 1912 and also boasts more than 100 Oscars for classics spanning from The Godfather to Titanic, though the studio has not mirrored the same recent spate of Hollywood honours.
The studio was not nominated for any projects last year by the Academy. Its last win came in 2022 with Top Gun: Maverick.
The deal with US states aims to ensure the merged studios will produce "real, robust movies" that will generate economic activity and put people back to work, said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the lawsuit and settlement.
To prevent the studio from fulfilling its annual quota with low-budget or automated content, the deal includes strict guardrails against "AI-generated" films.
As part of the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year. If it fails to meet its annual production quota, it will be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax, the film company founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein and his brother Bob.
Paramount also must ensure 20% of all film production takes place in the US for the first two years, rising to more than 30% through the following three years.

b1c653a4a82f.text: A new crop of powerful, Western open-weight AI systems are mounting a comeback, with fresh models from Reflection and Mistral narrowing China's recent lead. Why it matters: These models and others will give businesses and governments alternatives to the closed ecosystems of OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as to Chinese options they may have eschewed for security reasons. But putting powerful model weights into the world also makes their safeguards easier to remove, a concern that's growing as models become more capable in areas like cybersecurity. What they're saying: Both companies are arguing that raw intelligence isn't the only way to measure the AI race, and they present the notion of user control as a core opportunity and selling point. "Once you're spending that amount on intelligence, you want to move from renting it to owning it yourself," Reflection CEO Misha Laskin told Axios. "That's kind of where open source is very powerful because it is customizable at every level." Mistral VP of science Pierre Stock said the themes he repeatedly hears from customers include control over data and intellectual property, business continuity, the ability to customize models and cost. "I don't want to live in the future in which any oligopoly controls closed access to this type of intelligence," Stock said in an interview. Zoom in: Reflection on Monday introduced Beam, a 501-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, with 23 billion parameters active at a time. Reflection says Beam is competitive with China's GLM-5.2 and approaches Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-Max on some coding and agentic tasks. Its own published benchmarks show a mixed picture: Beam beats or roughly matches the Chinese models on some tests while trailing them on others. Reflection says Beam can achieve reasoning performance comparable to GLM-5.2 with three to four times less computing firepower — an important consideration because the cost of running AI models is now as important to many customers as raw performance. Reflection plans to release Beam's weights later this month, along with tools for running, evaluating and fine-tuning it. Meanwhile, Mistral said Tuesday it is finishing work on a new flagship model, Mistral Large 4, aka "Le Chonk." It's a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model with 49 billion active parameters, trained on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months in Mistral's own European data centers. Stock told Axios the company believes Le Chonk is the world's best open-weight model and said it can outperform closed models on certain tasks. But Stock acknowledged that Mistral hasn't yet caught the leading closed models. "We're not there yet on the frontier," he said. Mistral is initially making the model available through a moderated API, with a version with fewer restrictions and broader cybersecurity capabilities being shared with select partners for testing. It plans to release the weights Oct. 27 after further reinforcement learning and safety testing. The big picture: Chinese companies including Alibaba, Z.ai, Moonshot and DeepSeek have driven much of the recent momentum in open-weight AI. The arrival of competitive models from Reflection and Mistral suggests Western labs may be narrowing a gap that had begun to look structural. Yes, but: The same characteristic that gives customers control over an open-weight model also limits the developer's control over how it is used. Once weights are publicly available, users can modify the model, including attempting to remove safeguards added by its creator. That's particularly significant as models become more capable at cybersecurity and other potentially dangerous tasks. The other side: Mistral and Reflection argue that openness can also improve safety. Laskin said having a larger ecosystem able to inspect models and hunt for vulnerabilities is safer than concentrating that work among a few hundred researchers inside closed labs. He said there should nevertheless be capability-based safety thresholds that determine whether any model — open or closed — should be released. Stock acknowledged a trade-off in releasing weights but argued that making capable models available can accelerate cyber defenses and allow outside researchers to audit the technology. Mistral is using a staged release to give itself additional time for testing. Open-weight models also ensure that those defending against cyberattacks have adequate tools. "If we open weight as many models as possible, including ML4 — which is among the best models in the world on cyber — then you accelerate the defense part way more," Stock said.

87a117674832.text:
The bare-throated bellbird is loud. Very, very loud.
The explosive, metallic mating call of the snow-white male — a stout bird with a broad bill and distinctive blue-green throat patch — can top 130 decibels, louder than a jackhammer or a front-row seat at a Counting Crows concert.
That makes this South American forest dweller a contender for the title of world’s loudest bird. And now researchers think they know how it and other avian loudmouths produce such eardrum-rattling vocalizations.
Bigger bodies and, especially, wider beaks help these feathered screamers belt it out, behavioral ecologists João Menezes and Jeff Podos of the University of Massachusetts Amherst report September 29 in Evolution.
But what pushed some birds to evolve such volume in the first place remains a mystery. The researchers looked at mating behavior, habitat density and flight ability, but found no explanation that consistently held across species. “We weren’t able to find an overarching pattern that applies to birds in general,” Menezes says.
The quest to understand these sonic extremes dates back to 2019. That is when Podos and a colleague crowned the white bellbird (Procnias albus), an Amazonian cousin of the bare-throated bellbird (P. nudicollis), as a record-setting vocal powerhouse. Its 125-decibel calls were the loudest bird calls ever measured at the time.
Beyond the attention-grabbing number, the finding raised a broader question: What makes some birds so extraordinarily loud?
The honk of a Canada goose, for example, can reach chainsaw volume (100 decibels), while the chatter of a starling rarely rises above a dishwasher-level hum (70 decibels) — and ornithologists have surprisingly little understanding of why. Although scientists have spent decades cataloging the timing and frequency of birdsong, hoping to decode what birds are saying, the sheer loudness of bird voices has gone largely unexplored.
To get a read on the racket, Podos lugged a high-grade sound meter, the kind used to monitor noise levels in industrial workplaces, and a laser rangefinder into the woods, swamps and open fields around his home in western Massachusetts. He measured the calls of whatever birds he could find — warblers, sparrows, robins and more.
After logging a few dozen species, he enlisted Menezes, a then-grad student who at the time had recently joined his lab, to help turn the collection into a broader evolutionary analysis. Menezes measured bird vocalizations across his home country of Brazil, from the Atlantic Forest near São Paulo to the mountains surrounding Rio de Janeiro and beyond. He captured everything from the soft chirps of the dusky-throated hermit hummingbird to the piercing yelps of the red-legged seriema, a shaggy type of grassland bird.
All told, he and Podos compiled vocal volume data on 123 species, creating what they say is the largest such dataset to date.
The heftier the bird, the louder its call tended to be, and the same went for birds with broader beaks — a connection between anatomy and acoustic performance that biophysicist Gabriel Mindlin from the University of Buenos Aires in Argentina finds “sensible and plausible.”
“Larger birds have the potential to generate greater respiratory pressures and flows, while morphological features such as beak opening can affect how efficiently acoustic energy radiates,” says Mindlin, who studies birdsong but was not involved in the work.
Why evolution cranked up the volume on these avian megaphones, though, is a puzzle that remains, for now, unhatched.

682117814f1b.text: Scratch the surface of the year's biggest stories — the Iran war and AI — and both are bound up in the costs of energy . Why it matters: Prices for gasoline, diesel and power are playing a prominent role in some of the tightest races for control of Congress. The war has kept gasoline prices way above $4 per gallon for months, and helped push diesel to record highs. Fairly or unfairly, data centers are getting blamed for rising electricity prices . It's all unfolding as affordability more broadly tops the agenda in races nationwide. Here's a look at how energy politics are playing out in five critical contests... Senate Michigan. Power prices climbed faster than the national average over the past year in the Wolverine state, and data centers surfaced early in the Democratic primary and stayed prominent in the tight general election race. Former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers' campaign shows how Republican hopefuls are willing to split with President Trump on energy and AI — or at least get ahead of him. Rogers called for a one-year moratorium on data centers in August. And he called for a temporary ban on diesel exports in September, an idea Trump then flirted with but backed off. On the Democratic side, if Abdul El-Sayed's January "terms of engagement" for data centers looks familiar, it's because it reflects an increasingly common Democratic view around community buy-in and clean energy. Ohio. AI's voracious appetite for electricity is fueling the clash between Republican Sen. Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown. Husted has made the case that data centers — not households — should pay for the new power plants and grid infrastructure needed to serve them. A bill he sponsored aimed at doing that fell short in the Senate after passing the House overwhelmingly. Brown is attacking Husted for previously championing data centers and tax incentives to attract them to Ohio. The fight encapsulates a broader question surrounding the AI boom: Who should pay for the massive buildout needed to power it? Alaska. The Iran war is turning energy prices into a potent issue in the race between Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola. In rural communities, fuel already costs far more than in the Lower 48, with gasoline reaching $10 a gallon in some places. Peltola is tying rising fuel costs directly to Sullivan's support for the war, arguing higher diesel prices are hammering fishermen and families. Sullivan has called for temporarily halting U.S. diesel exports and argues Alaska should produce more of its own energy. Looming over it all is Trump's push for a massive Alaska project to export liquefied natural gas. House Colorado 8th. This is a contest where energy could be the tipping point. Both general elections in the district's young history have been decided by less than 1%, and energy is prominent this time around. One thing to watch is how much political cover a recent data center vote gives incumbent Republican Gabe Evans. Evans' bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act passed the House 417-3 last month. It urges states — but doesn't force them — to set rules ensuring data center developers cover generation and grid upgrade costs Don't sleep on gasoline either. New Democratic ads supporting challenger Manny Rutinel tie Evans to Trump's war with Iran and higher gasoline prices. Pennsylvania 8th. Data centers have become a central issue in the House race between Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan and Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti. Northeastern Pennsylvania is fielding proposals for the energy-hungry facilities. Cognetti is campaigning explicitly against projects that raise electric bills, threaten water supplies or receive tax breaks. Bresnahan, who has previously supported data center development, has introduced legislation aimed at protecting local governments that reject projects from corporate lawsuits. The fight captures the emerging politics around AI infrastructure: Communities may want the investment and jobs, but they also want control over the costs.
