Ghanaian authorities have arrested seven people for allegedly using banknotes to make so-called "money bouquets" and decorate cakes.
The Bank of Ghana says the practice is illegal and amounts to misuse and improper handling of the cedi, the national currency.
The arrests, carried out in collaboration with the police, followed a tip-off that led to a swoop on the suspects, all women, accused of selling the bouquets in different parts of the capital, Accra.
The arrests are the biggest enforcement of the law against misusing the currency. In July, the bank issued a notice warning this could amount to an offence.
It warned against "acts that tend to depreciate or impair the national currency, including any conduct that undermines its lawful value or use".
Bouquets of banknotes or cakes decorated with currency are often ordered as gifts for weddings, birthdays, graduations and other celebrations.
The police have launched investigations, and the authorities say the suspects will be prosecuted. They could face a fine or jail term, to be determined by the court.
Dinah Bonzi, an official in the Bank of Ghana's currency department, said anyone aiding or promoting such activities could also be arrested and prosecuted.
''The Ghana cedi is legal tenderâ¦ and must be treated with respect. The misuse or abuse of the currency is an offence and may attract sanctions under the law,'' she said.
"Today's arrest should serve as a clear warning to the public. Let us all handle the Ghana cedi with dignity."
The central bank has repeatedly warned against activities such as "spraying" - or throwing money at events such as weddings - writing on or altering notes and using them in decorations such as floral-like bouquets in weddings, birthdays and other occasions.
The use of money decorations has become more common in Ghana in recent years, with the practice also gaining a foothold in other African countries.
In recent years authorities in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and Botswana have also issued warnings against misusing the national currencies.

a1a78fa75700.text: By — Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/alito-says-supreme-court-cant-stem-rise-of-emergency-appeals-not-pleased-with-trumps-rhetoric Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Alito says Supreme Court can't stem rise of emergency appeals, 'not pleased' with Trump's rhetoric Politics Oct 6, 2026 10:25 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito says the escalating volume of emergency appeals before the court isn't a good thing, but he adds there's little the court can do to change the trajectory. The number of petitions asking the justices to intervene quickly has skyrocketed during President Donald Trump's second administration, putting the court at the center of hotly debated issues such as the Republican president's new ballroom construction and his proposed restrictions on mail ballots in the midterm elections. READ MORE: Supreme Court ready to tackle climate, immigration and gun rights. Here are 5 cases to watch The number of emergency applications now rivals the annual tally of cases the justices consider with full briefing and oral arguments, Alito wrote in a new book released Tuesday. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The justice told The Associated Press in a rare interview that the rhetoric about the court from Trump and his administration doesn't sit well with him. "I personally am not pleased with that," he said. "Everybody in this country has the right to criticize what we do. The substance of their criticism can be quite harsh. If we deserve it, then that's fine. But rhetoric is a different story." Alito spoke in connection with his first book, "So Ordered: An Originalist's View of The Constitution, The Court and Our Country." Coming 20 years after he was confirmed to the court after his nomination by President George W. Bush, a Republican, the book is a collection of speeches the 76-year-old has given over the years on religious liberty, his judicial philosophy and constitutional rights. Alito calls it 'offensive' to cast his opinions as MAGA Alito is perhaps best known for writing the decision that reversed Roe v. Wade and ended abortion as a nationwide right, and he has been one of the most consistent members of the court's conservative bloc. He's also voted in favor of some of Trump's signature policies, even those the rest of the conservative wing has struck down. But he rejects the idea that his decisions are in the "Make America Great Again" camp. READ MORE: Supreme Court lets Trump continue deporting people to 3rd countries while justices consider policy "It's offensive," he said. "I honestly try to decide every single case on the merits, every single application on the merit. And that's true whether the president is Donald Trump or Joe Biden or Barack Obama or anybody else." Trump, for his part, has cheered Alito as "one of the Greatest of All Time" even as he maligned justices whom he appointed as "unpatriotic" and "merely a shell of their original selves." Alito said the harsh rhetoric from across the spectrum doesn't affect how the justices rule but does play a role in the public's declining trust in the court. "The terms used by presidents and by members of their administration, Cabinet officers, other high-ranking officers in describing the Supreme Court and their decisions, and sometimes individual justices, is far different from what we saw 15 years ago," Alito said. Much of the president's frustration has come after the court ruled against him on some of his central initiatives, including tariffs and birthright citizenship. Those decisions have been handed down after months of consideration, including oral arguments. Surge in court's emergency decisions is likely 'going to continue' In emergency decisions, by contrast, the president has a much stronger track record of wins. Typically made in days or weeks, emergency orders are designed to be temporary, lasting only as cases continue to play out in lower courts. But since that process can take years, those decisions can still have important real-world consequences. Critics, including Alito's liberal-leaning colleague Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, have complained about the court's recent handling of the emergency docket and outlined proposed steps the justices could take. Alito, though, said there's little the court can do to stem the tide. Presidents have increasingly used executive orders to enact their policies rather than passing laws through Congress, leading to lawsuits and "robust" decisions from lower-court judges that send a case quickly to the Supreme Court, he said. "Unless something changes there, and I don't foresee it right now, I'm afraid this is going to continue," he said. "An application is something that I think we have to rule on." Alito says recusal from climate change case wasn't required but a 'judgment call' Alito also detailed his decision to step away from hearing a climate change case that opened the term. Dozens of similar lawsuits have been filed on whether cities can sue oil and gas companies over damage linked to global warming. Billions of dollars could be at stake, a potentially serious threat to the industry, according to court documents. Alito had faced calls to recuse himself because he owns stock in oil companies. He told the AP that the stock came from an inheritance his wife received from her father that she doesn't want to sell. b048af565708.text: California leaders blasted President Trump after he said during a Monday rally about Iran , "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego." The big picture: The backlash — and the White House's insistence that Trump was misunderstood — underscored the ambiguity of his meandering speech: An argument that the war was worth enduring to protect Americans came out sounding like an invitation to attack two U.S. cities. An administration account posted on X that Trump meant that the U.S. was fighting Iran to "STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego." Driving the news: Faced with an unpopular war and stubbornly high gas prices, Trump seemingly argued that the current economic pain is "a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe" during his Nebraska rally. "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe," he said. "They can take out a city. Let them take, let it — let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That's — this is a very small price to pay, and it's gonna be over very soon." Friction point: The comment received swift backlash from Golden State leaders: California Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote , "After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego. He is deranged and dangerous." San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria also admonished the president, writing, "San Diego is not collateral damage. We are not expendable." And LA Mayor Karen Bass responded , "His statements against our city are dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety. The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives." Between the lines: Analysts online perceived his comments in various ways, with some noting his circuitous language could have masked his true intent. But others reeled at the plain text of the comments from the president, who in the past has suggested using "dangerous" U.S. cities as military "training grounds." The White House pointed Axios to a post from Communications Director Steven Cheung, who argued the president "was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped. Context: Military bases across San Diego employ more than 136,000 active duty members and civilians, according to a 2025 report from the San Diego Military Advisory Council. Rep. Scott Peters (D), who represents the city, noted those deep military roots in his statement condemning the president's words, writing, "San Diego is a proud military town, home to 115,000 courageous active duty servicemembers and their families. Military service is at the root of our community and culture." Go deeper: After nixing Iran proposal, Trump tells Axios he expects talks this week

Lizâs view
The keys to succeeding on Wall Street are to a) make money and b) make money differently than others. Performance is table stakes; outperformance gets you the glory.
AI is messing with that logic. Nvidiaâs $500 billion consortium includes the four largest alternative-asset managers in the world and six of the top eight. Blackstone and Apollo are jointly providing billions of dollars for Anthropic to buy compute. Anthropicâs AI-for-the-real-world consultancy offshoot raised $1.5 billion from Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, Goldman Sachs, General Atlantic, Leonard Green, and Apollo. Nearly every big private-equity firm not on that list is backing OpenAIâs competing version. (Goldman, being Goldman, is in both.) Here is a handy chart.
This is not how things usually work on Wall Street, where the goal is to snake investments away from rivals, not share them. The last time private equity clubbed up on deals too big for any one of them to handle solo, we got some of the worst buyouts in history.
Some of the crowding can be explained by the sheer amount of money needed. âWhy can you get five or six of the leading players at one table? Because thereâs enough to go around,â Brookfield Asset Management CEO Connor Teskey told me last week. He thinks there will still be winners and losers in the AI trade as investors stake out corners within it; Brookfield has made bets on sovereign AI in Europe, Blue Owl is an AI landlord, Apollo is a lender willing to take on chip risk.
But whether those are different bets or marketing gloss for the same big bet is less clear to me. AI is starting to look like an âIBGYBGâ trade, a Wall Street phrase that made it into the US governmentâs postmortem report on the 2008 subprime crash: âIâll be gone, youâll be gone.â Everyone wins if it works, even if nobody looks like a standout genius. Everyone loses if it doesnât, but nobody looks like a standout moron.
The irony is that the investing world was just returning to a place where outperformance seemed possible again when AI arrived. Two decades of easy money had made everyone look like undifferentiated geniuses. A more fractured, risky, and dynamic world of wars, inflation, and tariffs might have encouraged investors to zig where others zagged. âI think weâll start to see the pull of groupthink become a little weaker, and contrarianism start to pay off,â I wrote in early 2024. Rubio hailed the role of diplomacy in resolving conflicts as he began a three-nation tour of NATO allies in the capital of Iceland, where concerns over the Republican administration's often brusque and sometimes rude approach to traditional friends and partners have stirred unease. However, both Rubio and Gunnarsdóttir downplayed differences between the allies and said both countries were committed to deepening and expanding military and commercial ties. Rubio made clear that the United States would not do anything in Iceland without Iceland's consent. He noted that priorities have shifted again. And, he went out of his way to praise Iceland: "We have tremendous respect for the people. We have respect for the country in the role it plays, and it has for a very long time," he said. Iceland's unease persists Iceland has been uneasy about Trump's intentions toward it after the posting of a map showing the colors of the U.S. flag sprawling across all of North America and extending to Iceland and Greenland. The unease has persisted despite an agreement reached last month to increase the U.S. presence in the neighboring Danish territory of Greenland that appears to have ended Trump's earlier demand for the U.S. to take full control. But on Tuesday, after Rubio's talks with Gunnarsdóttir and Iceland's Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir, those tensions appeared to be on the wane. "We remain focused on the future," she said. Rubio, meanwhile, said he was not in Iceland to talk about social media posts. "Everything is very positive," he said. Rubio talks up 'shared priorities' Before leaving Washington on Monday, Rubio said the visit is intended to "advance our shared priorities: a secure Arctic, stronger commercial and energy ties, and closer defense cooperation." He offered no hint of tensions with the island that, while a NATO member, has no standing army. The map incident, however, alarmed Icelanders, and in response, Gunnarsdóttir summoned U.S. Ambassador Billy Long to a meeting at which she made it clear the post was unacceptable. He has since apologized for the quip. Long is not the first Trump ambassador to Iceland to have raised concerns with the host government. In Trump's first term, Ambassador Jeffrey Ross Gunter left locals in relatively crime-free Reykjavik aghast over his request to hire armed bodyguards, which prompted complaints. A lawyer for one of the seven men accused of participating in a Cornell University gang rape has called for the special prosecutor on the case to recuse herself over past public comments.
The lawyer had said a social media post from New York Attorney General Letitia James throws into question her investigation's "integrity and independence".
In the 28 September post, James wrote that "what this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable" and told survivors that "we stand with you".
The university's administration is under fire over its alleged mishandling of the October 2024 incident and, according to US media, now faces a no-confidence vote by Cornell faculty.
The university's Faculty Senate, a governing body comprised of professors and other academic staff, will vote on a resolution of no confidence next week, according to reports.
A majority no-confidence vote would be a largely symbolic gesture, signalling the broader faculty's discontent and applying pressure on university leadership to act.
The BBC has reached out to Cornell University for comment.
Allegations made in a lawsuit against seven men and the Ivy League university have rocked the campus in New York state, with hundreds of students and faculty members gathering there on Monday in protest, and sparked anger across the country.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul last week appointed James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case and how law enforcement and the university initially responded to the allegations made by a woman identified in the lawsuit as Jane Doe.
Jane Doe has accused the university of failing to protect her, after she was allegedly drugged and raped by the men for several hours at a fraternity party.
Days before she was appointed special prosecutor, James wrote on X: "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable.
"I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers," she continued. "To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you."
The lawyer for one of the seven accused said these remarks were disqualifying.
In a statement sent to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the lawyer said her comments conflict with the need for "independently evaluating the evidence".
"This is not an accusation that Attorney General James is corrupt, acting in bad faith or incapable of performing her duties professionally," the statement said.
"Nor am I suggesting that a court has determined that she is legally disqualified. The point is much narrower: an avoidable question now hangs over this investigation, and voluntary recusal would remove it."
Governor Hochul and James were questioned about impartiality concerns during a news conference, and Hochul said James would "follow the facts".
"She'll examine the evidence and go wherever it leads, and if the evidence supports charges, she will pursue them," Hochul said.

US televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar media empire before being jailed for fraud and conspiracy, has died aged 86.
Bakker and his then-wife Tammy Faye founded a Christian television programme called The PTL Club in 1974, which at its peak attracted 13 million viewers per day.
The 86-year-old's death was announced on Monday by his second wife Lori Bakker, who described him as "a pioneer of Christian television".
By the late 80s, Bakker and Tammy Faye's empire began to fall apart after he became embroiled in a sex scandal and later convicted of mail and wire fraud. Tammy Faye, who divorced him in 1992, was never charged.
Bakker remarried in 1998, and alongside second wife Lori launched a new TV ministry in 2003.
Lori Bakker described her late husband as "my best friend, and the man I was honoured to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry".
She did not specify the cause of death.
However, Bakker's first program The PTL Club - short for 'Praise the Lord' or 'People That Love' - was what cemented his fame with his first wife Tammy Faye.
The couple built their empire with 2,000 employees and a 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA theme park complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina.
The Bakkers had a famously opulent lifestyle, owning a private jet, multiple homes, luxury cars, jewellery and even an air-conditioned dog house.
In 1987, Bakker resigned from the PTL ministry after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with a former church secretary Jessica Hahn.
It later emerged Hanhn received a $265,000 payoff with ministry funds, resulting in Bakker being defrocked of his ministerial credentials and right to perform religious duties.
Hahn also accused Bakker of sexual assault, though the evangelist denied this, claiming the encounter had been consensual.
Bakker was then convicted in 1989 of 24 counts of mail and wire fraud and conspiracy in a scheme involving their Christian theme park, and served more than four years in prison.
Tammy Faye stayed with her husband throughout the trial but divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. She died of cancer in 2007.
Following Bakker's release from prison in 1994, he wrote a book titled I Was Wrong and married his second wife Lori in 1998.
The couple began a TV ministry together in 2003 and in 2008 they began taping The Jim Bakker Show.

Situated next to Nigeria, the small west African country of Benin is generally used to being left in the shadows of its footballing powerhouse neighbour.
But the Cheetahs are about to have their own moment in the limelight.
On Tuesday (Wednesday 00:00 BST), Benin face Argentina in Buenos Aires for what will be Lionel Messi's final international match.
A specially designed Argentina kit has been created to mark the occasion - and the shirt worn by Messi could go on to become one of the most expensive ever.
The historic fixture will see the World Cup runners-up take on players who ply their trade in Finland, Switzerland's second tier and the South African Premiership.
'I've had to buy my own plane ticket'
One of Benin's best-known players is their captain, Steve Mounie.
The forward plays for German Bundesliga side FC Augsburg, but will also be known to Huddersfield Town fans having played for the club between 2017-2020.
He's been a regular with the national side for more than a decade but says he's never played a game for them outside of Africa.
"When the coach called me and told me about this game. We didn't know it was going to be the last game of Leo Messi," Mounie told BBC Sport.
"It was like the cherry on top of the cake. It adds some more values to this big event for Benin, and it's going to be a big event for the world of football."
However, injury means Mounie will play no part in the game. Instead of staying at home recovering, however, he says this was not a moment he could miss out on.
"I cannot play," he said. "I just came to join the team, to support the team. And, I need to be honest with this because football is my passion. I came for myself.
"I even paid for my own ticket to come here.
"I would prefer to be on the bench, but if they tell me that I need to be in the stand, I will be in the stand. There is no problem, but I want to see the game from a pitch view."
The former Premier League striker says, while the result of the friendly is largely inconsequential, those players who are selected will know it's a great chance to enhance their reputations and that of Beninese football.
"We are a team that is very disciplined," said Mounie. "We have a lot of young talent in the team right now that have good technical skills. We are always willing to go forward. We play pressing football, but when we cannot, we stick together and we fight.
"We are a team like a family, And I think we can relate to this Argentina team because they feel like they are like a family too, which Messi is a father to."
'Every player on the pitch is looking to swap with him'
Argentina warmed up for the fixture against Benin by defeating fellow west African side Burkina Faso 7-0.
Many will be predicting a similar scoreline this game - and it's unlikely Messi will play the full 90 minutes.
A more likely scenario is that, with Argentina a few goals to the good, Messi will be substituted in the second half, allowing the sold-out crowd at Estadio Monumental to say farewell to their country's greatest sports star.
Once the final whistle does go - don't be surprised if there's a rush towards the World Cup-winning captain.
"To get hold of a Messi match-worn shirt is incredibly tough because everybody knows how valuable they are," said Doug Bierton, founder of Classic Football Shirts.
"So every player on the pitch is looking to swap with him. It's the first time a legend has bowed out with a special edition shirt."
Bierton, whose private collection of iconic football shirts reaches into the thousands, says the last match-worn Messi shirt would be collector's dream.
He ranks it in the same category as Diego Maradona's shirt worn when he scored his 'Hand of God' goal against England at the 1986 World Cup. A jersey which sold for Â£7.1m in an auction in May 2022.
Another item considered in that realm is Zinedine Zidane's shirt from the last time he played for France - which ended in a red card after being sent off for headbutting Italy's Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup final.
The fact Messi's shirt is being worn in a friendly - yet considered in such high regard - is perhaps testament to the belief he is the greatest footballer ever.
So Bierton predicts it won't be just Benin players who will be after the jersey.
"I'm sure some of his team-mates will be too, he's good friends with [Rodrigo] De Paul," he said. "He'll probably be after it as well. Does he get a gift, a retirement present?
"The kit man will be after it. Who knows? I'm literally going to watch the match just to see who he swaps shirts with."

4e4085296cdc.text: By — Jim Salter, Associated Press Jim Salter, Associated Press By — Hallie Golden, Associated Press Hallie Golden, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/jim-bakker-minister-who-built-a-televangelism-empire-and-lost-it-from-sex-and-money-scandals-dies-at-86 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Jim Bakker, minister who built a televangelism empire and lost it from sex and money scandals, dies at 86 Nation Oct 6, 2026 11:27 AM EDT Jim Bakker, who built a huge TV following and evangelical empire with his first wife, Tammy Faye, which later collapsed in a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86. Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. The cause of death was not provided. "He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry," she said. READ MORE: Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84 The pair lived near Branson, an entertainment destination in Missouri, where they had filmed their TV show "The Jim Bakker Show" since its launch in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020. But it was the "The PTL Club," which at its peak in the mid-1980s drew 13 million nightly TV viewers, that made Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker cultural icons — so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 90s by late-night comedians and parodied on "Saturday Night Live." The couple also built Heritage USA, a Christian theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina, and a movie about their lives, "The Eyes of Tammy Faye," was released in September 2021. Bakker starts out as a traveling preacher Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry. He preached and she sang and played the accordion in churches and tent revivals across the country. They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children's show on Robertson's Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, Bakker was hosting "The 700 Club," a Christian talk show. READ MORE: Televangelist Jimmy Swaggart, whose massive ministry was toppled by prostitution scandals, dies at 90 Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. "The PTL Club" — PTL stands for "Praise the Lord" — became its signature show. In its heyday in the 1980s, "The PTL Club" attracted millions of viewers and brought in millions of dollars annually. The show featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye — charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara — sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina. They were often parodied by TV comedians, mocked for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye's abundant makeup. Sex scandal and financial crimes damage his empire Their standing began to crumble in March 1987, when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Hahn alleged that Bakker sexually assaulted her; Bakker maintained that the encounter was consensual. Bakker was forced to resign from his empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell. Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often seen with mascara-stained tears running down her face. Bakker was indicted in 1988 for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL's finances. He was convicted the following year and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison. The sentence was later reduced to eight years. At a news conference after he was found guilty, Tammy Faye sang the hymn, "On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand." Their marriage fell apart and Tammy Faye divorced the still-incarcerated Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison. Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007. Bakker was released on parole in 1994 and married Lori in 1998. They launched "The Jim Bakker Show" on the PTL Satellite Network five years later. In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic. The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March 2020. Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and Lori Bakker adopted five children in 2002. Salter, a former Associated Press journalist, was the main author of this obituary. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 156bfc893e2b.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press By — Rebecca Santana, Associated Press Rebecca Santana, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/kilmar-abrego-garcia-is-set-to-be-back-in-court-as-he-battles-deportation-to-liberia Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Kilmar Ábrego Garcia is set to be back in court as he battles deportation to Liberia Politics Oct 6, 2026 11:08 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Kilmar Ábrego Garcia on Tuesday will be back in federal court, where the federal government will continue its attempt to deport him in an 18-month saga that began when he was mistakenly sent to El Salvador last year. The government is moving to vacate a preliminary injunction put in place by U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis preventing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from detaining and deporting Ábrego Garcia to the West African country of Liberia. His legal team is seeking to make the injunction permanent. The judge left previous orders in place last December and ordered him released from custody. READ MORE: Justice Department attempting to revive criminal case against Kilmar Abrego Garcia The Salvadoran national's case became a focal point in the immigration debate after he was mistakenly deported to his home country last year. Since his return, he has been fighting a second deportation to an African country as proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Ábrego Garcia argued that if he were going to be deported, it should be to Costa Rica, which previously agreed to take him. But Todd Lyons, the former acting director of ICE, said in a March 2026 memo that deporting Ábrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be "prejudicial to the United States," because the U.S. had expended resources and political capital negotiating with Liberia to accept third-country nationals. The push for deportation to Liberia continued even after the U.S. signed an agreement with Costa Rica to accept deportees who cannot legally be returned to their home countries. READ MORE: Congressional Democrats to investigate efforts to deport U.S. military members and their families "The government is leading the same rodeo as many times before. Sending Kilmar to Costa Rica is on the table. However, the government continues to punish him for pursuing his constitutional rights and seeks to ship him to Liberia," said Jossie Flor Sapunar, the national communications director for We Are CASA, an activist group that has supported Ábrego Garcia and his family and intends to be at the courthouse. "Kilmar has become an international symbol of due process, a symbol which the Trump administration wants to silence." She added in an email that the family deserves privacy, either at home in Maryland or in Costa Rica. Ábrego Garcia, 31, has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. He was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 after picking up his then-5-year-old son, who has autism and other disabilities, from his grandmother's house, according to court papers. READ MORE: 'A perfect tool for abuse.' Why experts are concerned about ICE's $17 million electric shock gloves contract Ábrego Garcia was then sent to a mega-prison in El Salvador known as CECOT, which activists say is rife with abuses and where inmates are packed into cells and never allowed outside. ICE officials admitted in court filings that his deportation there was an "administrative error." Facing public pressure and a court order, President Donald Trump's Republican administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May 2026, finding that the Justice Department's pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Ábrego Garcia for challenging his deportation. A Mother’s Brain
Susana Carmona
MIT Press, $27.95
When it comes to new motherhood, the baby typically takes center stage, garnering most of people’s attention. But in a refreshing twist, neuroscientist Susana Carmona shifts the spotlight to the mom. In the opening pages of A Mother’s Brain, Carmona cheerfully tells us, “here, we’ll hardly discuss babies at all.” Mothers are her protagonists.
What follows is a captivating, passionate and well-grounded journey through the fascinating process of “matrescence.” A word coined to echo “adolescence,” another time of seismic changes, matrescence includes the intense reorganization a woman’s brain undergoes as she becomes a mom. So far, early studies have revealed a sculpting of brain circuits (and Carmona is quick to point out that less can be more), heightened social instincts and perhaps even a boost of resilience during old age.
This mom found the book to be a treasure trove of motherly delights. Scientific concepts are woven with social and cultural strands, from the poignant to the weird to the profound. Certain passages in the book allowed me the pleasure of relistening to the song “The Mother” by Brandi Carlile, in which she sings, “Welcome to the end of being alone inside your mind.” A Mother’s Brain also kindly pointed me to the viral video, “Mother Rat Saves Baby from Snake.”
As one of the foremost scientists studying matrescence, Carmona is an authoritative guide through the latest research, of which there is a dismayingly small amount. Still, the book covers scientific ground including hormones, evolution and brain networks. History, social constructs and the pressures of modern life come into the story, too.
If you prefer a light read, Carmona will occasionally warn you when a section is scientifically dense. Then she will invite you along anyway. “But if you do like hormones — well, we’re going to have fun,” Carmona writes at the beginning of a chapter. And it was fun. I was shocked to learn, for instance, just how massive the hormonal upheaval during pregnancy is. The amount of estrogen that floods a woman’s body, including her brain, during the 40 weeks of pregnancy is more than that of the amount that would otherwise accumulate over her entire fertile life, which lasts 35 years on average.
Along the way, Carmona thoughtfully addresses scientific puzzlers such as this: Mothers often report feeling less mentally sharp, yet laboratory studies show almost no neurological decline. Attributed to “mommy brain” or “momnesia,” mental slips might be due to a lack of sleep, or a shifting of attention, or even just an expectation.
This pervasive, negative stereotype of “mommy brain” can then build on itself, getting stronger as women buy into the incorrect idea that motherhood leaves them dumber. If a woman expects her memory to get worse, she’ll see signs of it in even normal mistakes. “I have watched brilliant women grow so insecure about their intelligence on becoming mothers that they abandon the projects that were once vital to them,” Carmona writes. Assumptions about their diminished brainpower can lead women to pull back from valuable parts of their lives. “It matters — a lot — how we talk to ourselves about these things.”
As a mother herself, Carmona brings her experiences into the narrative. It couldn’t be any other way. “Motherhood is lived,” she writes. “It happens in your gut, your identity, your core.”
At its heart, this book is a love letter to moms, who have been invisible to the scientific gaze for too long. It’s time to write a new tale of matrescence, Carmona argues. “A story that recognizes mothers as the essence of the human species, the carriers of knowledge about how we create bonds — and, through them, society and culture.”
By putting the intense and wild changes of motherhood into words, Carmona offers us a powerful and necessary story.

Timâs view
As Russia again ramps up its attacks on Ukraineâs electricity grid ahead of the winter heating season, this time Kyiv has a new ally in its corner: El NiÃ±o.
Last week, 8,000 households around Ukraine temporarily went dark after the Kremlinâs first large-scale grid attack since last winter. It was a disheartening preview of things to come: Just seven months ago, Ukrainians emerged from their harshest winter since the full-scale invasion, when relentless bombardment of energy plants and substations left many with no heat and few hours of daily power access for weeks at a time. This week, Russiaâs Defense Ministry made clear that more of the same is coming following a record campaign of strikes by Ukraineâs long-distance drones against Russian oil refineries in the past two months, which according to Kyiv have now taken out more than half of Russiaâs refining capacity. Ukraine has good reason to be worried: Moscowâs offensive position in the air war has improved since this time last year, with the deployment of jet-powered drones and a gaping deficit in Ukraineâs missile defense supplies.
But a number of factors are working in Ukraineâs favor. Western aid for rebuilding the energy sector continues to flow in; some $250 million in energy hardware is expected for delivery between now and February, according to European officials. Ukraine is entering the winter with a natural gas surplus it didnât have a year ago, and with a much higher share of its critical energy assets ensconced behind protective concrete barriers that are surprisingly effective at blunting damage from all but direct missile hits. More utility-scale renewables are online, and people and businesses across Ukrainian society have learned from successive bleak winters how to muddle through with batteries, generators, blankets, and candles.
Finally, and perhaps decisively, thereâs the weather. Last yearâs winter in Ukraine was the coldest in decades. Thatâs the factor that turns a blackout from an inconvenience to a deadly threat. This year, however, an exceptionally strong and possibly even record-breaking El NiÃ±o weather pattern â driven by warm ocean surface temperatures in the Pacific â is expected to make for a warm and wet winter in Europe. Thatâs good news for the EU, which is staring down a gas shortage. It could be problematic for Russia, which will also likely be warm but will be exposed to above-average food and fuel import prices. For Ukraine, itâs an asset. But Iâm still looking for an apartment with a working fireplace.

A month after Germany's far-right AfD scored a decisive victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, the party's candidate Tobias Rausch has been elected as parliament speaker there too.
Not since World War Two has a far-right party secured the post of speaker, and protesters outside the building in Magdeburg held up banners saying, "Never again is now".
Although the AfD fell three seats short of a majority in last month's election, Rausch, 35, comfortably won Tuesday's vote with the support of 9 MPs from other parties.
"The days of political firewalls should be a thing of the past," Rausch said after the vote, rejecting a post-war consensus in German politics not to work with the far right.
This was the first time since last month's state vote that Saxony-Anhalt's newly elected representatives had gathered in parliament, and regional Greens party leader Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz said "a line has been crossed" with the election of a far-right speaker of parliament, and it was a watershed moment.
"We will not let ourselves be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights are curtailed either here or for people in the state," she said.
The AfD is considered pro-Russian and anti-immigrant, with plans to segregate child refugees in schools, as well as intolerant towards the LGBT community.
Within Saxony-Anhalt it is also classed as "right-wing extremist" by domestic intelligence, a description rejected by party leaders. Until now its members have sat on the right fringe of the state parliament, but ahead of Tuesday's inaugural session it successfully argued that it should now sit in the centre.
Rausch, a trained estate agent, has been a member of the parliament for 10 years and he is seen as a close confidant of local AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund, a charismatic figure who is now seeking to become state premier in December.
His new role is largely symbolic, but Rausch will now chair debates, have the power to control access to the parliament building and represent parliament at official events.
Although his victory was secured by five MPs from the hard-left BSW, there was surprise that four other unidentified MPs also voted for Rausch. Commentators immediately asked if he had secured the backing of members of the conservative CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has ruled out working with the AfD.
Fourteen of the CDU's state MPs took part in the vote, but only five of them abstained as planned, and one unconfirmed report suggested four may have backed Rausch. Ahead of the vote, all 15 had ruled out voting for the AfD.
Outside parliament, more than 300 protesters voiced their anger at the AfD's victory, and they crowded around Ulrich Siegmund as he spoke to German media.
Siegmund's bid to become state premier is by no means secure. Like Rauch he will need the backing of 42 MPs in the 83-seat legislature.
The BSW has refused to enter into a coalition with the AfD and has said it would instead back a non-partisan candidate for state premier and abstain in December's vote.

It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (Â£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.
The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.
Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.
Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.
1. Streaming prices may rise
Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS.
Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time.
While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability.
The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings.
Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said viewers will undoubtedly get access to a bigger catalog.
But he told the BBC: "There's no way that a combined Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming service won't end up costing more for those who subscribe to only one of the services."
2. More film releases
As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger, Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years.
For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year.
That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must to be shown in cinemas.
The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year.
If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax â the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein.
Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date.
"Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said.
"Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift".
Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema.
As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas.
Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year.
3. Hollywood jobs could be hit
For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground.
Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods.
Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken".
"It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment, it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts."
A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years.
The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022.
Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities".
She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network."
Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts.
"Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added.
4. CNN and CBS could change
To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount.
The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN.
Both networks have faced intense political pressure - CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump - as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation.
Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson - the former director general of the BBC - to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News's editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role.
Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS.
Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom.
Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as "worthless".
"The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news," Stern said.
Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. "An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation," she said.

After Semafor reported last week that Chipotle had tapped bankers to fend off a potential takeover, we started digging to see who might take over the $40 billion burrito maker. People close to the company tell Semafor that Chipotle hasnât received a takeover bid, and weâre loath to peddle in deal rumors. But one theory that keeps coming up is notable, either because it highlights the dearth of good ideas out there or because itâs so out of left-field it just might bear entertaining: A Starbucks-Chipotle tie-up.
No, weâre not talking about a pumpkin spice burrito bowl (in fact, weâre begging Brian Niccol, the former Chipotle CEO who now runs Starbucks, not to go there.) But a Yum Brands-esque approach where â like KFC, Pizza Hut, and Taco Bell â the chains operate separately but combine their real-estate footprints and back-office operations makes sense on paper. Niccol worked at Yum for more than a decade and understands that scale matters in razor-thin restaurant margins. And Starbucks could provide a platform to grow Chipotleâs nascent international business. Starbucks declined to comment. Chipotle did not return a request for comment.
Of course, Starbucks would instantly rerate at a lower multiple if it pursued Chipotle, and would likely have to sell new stock to pay for it, further pressuring shares that are flat since Niccol took over in 2024. It would also require a pretty gutsy board of directors willing to make another bet on a CEO itâs still getting to know â and who has yet to prove out the turnaround strategy at his own company. There have been weirder marriages.
Notable
- Brian Niccol has an appetite for turnarounds, Semaforâs Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson wrote earlier this year. Before Starbucks, he was already at Chipotle, which he helped revive after a food poisoning crisis to deliver a near 800% share price surge.

8a249355b11c.text: Paramount Skydance on Tuesday closed its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, ending a dramatic, yearlong process that rattled Hollywood, Wall Street and Washington. Why it matters: The deal creates one of the largest entertainment behemoths in the world and makes David Ellison — a lesser-known figure outside of Hollywood — one of the most powerful people in culture and business. Zoom in: The combined entity, rebranded Skydance, will house three major movie studios (Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros. Pictures and Skydance), two global streamers (Paramount+ and HBO Max) and two major news networks (CNN and CBS). It will also create a cable juggernaut, marrying Paramount's Viacom channels, such as MTV, VH1 and Comedy Central, with WBD's cable networks, including TBS, TNT, Food Network and Discovery. The combination of those assets on the back end won't all be felt by consumers, but product changes are coming. The combined company, for example, plans to merge HBO Max and Paramount + into one giant unified streamer. The big picture: The transaction forced the entertainment industry and regulators around the world to confront how much consolidation is necessary for traditional media companies to compete with Big Tech. While some countries took a closer look at the deal than others, every government that required regulatory approval for the merger ultimately blessed the transaction. Although Netflix did meaningfully engage in a bidding war for WBD, it eventually abandoned its interest when the asset became too pricey. Reality check: Merger fights don't typically enter the zeitgeist for everyday Americans, but this one played into a broader societal debate around the concentration of power among the elite and the independence of federal regulators. Ellison's father, Oracle co-founder and Trump ally Larry Ellison , agreed to backstop billions of dollars of equity financing to seal the deal. Federal regulators cleared billions of dollars in equity investments from Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds to support the deal. The Federal Communications Commission, led by Trump ally Brendan Carr, granted Paramount's request to exceed foreign ownership limits for broadcasters. Between the lines: The political tension surrounding the deal was on full display when a dozen Democratic state attorneys general sued to block the transaction as it approached the finish line this summer. The state AGs said their case was rooted in traditional antitrust law around film and cable dominance, not politics. But after a settlement was announced clearing the deal, at least one participating state attorney general admitted that they wanted the agreement to force a divestiture of CBS and CNN. State of play: To alleviate regulatory concerns about the enormous concentration of assets, Skydance made a slew of commitments in its settlement, including theatrical film release minimums and investments in domestic production jobs. But the creative industry is still on edge as it anticipates a potentially huge number of job cuts as a result of the merger. What to watch: The deal, which is one of the most highly levered transactions in American history, will test the market's appetite for megamergers financed by huge amounts of debt amid rising interest rates. To get the transaction over the finish line, Paramount raised $52 billion in new debt, per Bloomberg . Some of that debt is very expensive, carrying a yield of nearly 9%. In addition to the debt it raised, Skydance will carry WBD's existing liabilities, totaling $87.5 billion in debt, according to Fitch Ratings . Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Christine Wang/Axios The bottom line: Ellison has proven himself to be one of the most savvy dealmakers in American history. His next test is whether he can build a sustainable business from a mountain of debt.

0f215707288f.text: Some companies are preparing for an AI-fueled chip squeeze that could push up prices far beyond the data center boom alone, Mary Daly, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, tells Axios. Why it matters: The Fed can usually look through supply shocks that come and go. Daly's concern is that AI, tariffs and higher energy costs could last longer than expected or compound each other — keeping inflation elevated and requiring more tightening. State of play: Daly says AI demand could spread beyond high-end chips before supply catches up, extending the shock beyond the period the Fed would normally expect to look through. "I see it less as a one-off," she says, referring to AI-driven pressure on chip and other technology prices. Daly says the Fed typically thinks in terms of shocks fading within one to three years. "This is probably further out before we get relief." "It doesn't seem like the demand for AI is going down. If anything, it seems like it's going up." Zoom in: Daly's district includes Silicon Valley and many of the companies driving the AI boom. In conversations with business contacts, she says, she's starting to hear signs that companies are bracing for tighter chip supplies — suggesting that the AI boom is beginning to alter purchasing and product-design decisions outside the data center sector. Daly says that some firms are seeking forward contracts for memory chips "so that they know they have a supplier." Those contracts can give companies more certainty about future supply — a notable development in the memory sector , a fast-depreciating market where firms typically have less reason to lock in chips ahead of time. Daly says some companies are also beginning to "reengineer their products" to rely less on chips, giving them more room to maneuver in case supplies tighten. "I see that as a signal that there is a little bit of concern this is going to spread more broadly." What to watch: The fear is that the scramble for AI hardware begins competing with the chips used in cars, appliances and other goods — recreating some of the bottlenecks that drove prices higher after the pandemic, Daly says. She points to autos after the pandemic, when chip shortages left manufacturers unable to finish vehicles and pushed prices higher. The risk now is that demand for AI-specific equipment spills into the broader semiconductor market, raising costs for companies with little connection to data centers. Friction point: The Fed could face an awkward problem as AI-driven price pressures spread. The companies fueling the boom are also among the least sensitive to higher interest rates. "These hyperscalers aren't very interest rate-sensitive," Daly says, though she notes they could become more so as they increasingly rely on borrowing to finance the AI buildout. Daly says the biggest AI spending numbers are concentrated among hyperscalers, but plenty of other companies investing in the technology are more sensitive to borrowing costs. That means higher rates can still restrain the broader economy and inflation outlook, even if they do less to slow the firms at the center of the boom. "I do think tightening policy has an effect on the outlook for inflation," Daly says. The bottom line: The AI boom is emerging as a fresh inflation risk for the Fed — one that could spread through supply chains, linger for years and prove more difficult to cool with higher interest rates. Daly affirmed her support for the Fed's interest rate hike three weeks ago, and, as has become the norm among top officials, declined to say much about whether she advocates further action. But she did give a sense of what will shape her view: whether the energy, trade and other shocks that have pushed up inflation this year show signs of abating. What they're saying: "I was very pleased, very supportive of the rate hike we took in September," Daly says. "It seemed completely necessary at this juncture to respond to the fact that inflation risks have gone up." "Whether more will be needed depends on the same set of conditions ... that I mentioned," she says. "If the shocks that we've experienced — tariffs, oil prices from the Middle East conflict, and then AI — if they prove to be conventional shocks where they come, they go, and they have temporary effects, then we may not need more. And I still have some probability on that." "But if they either compound each other or they just simply last longer than we had forecast that they would ... if we have a second round of tariff negotiations that result in more tariffs, then that would be a second shock on top of a first shock. That would extend the period of time over which those shocks would play out." She later added that the Fed's policy committee, the FOMC, is "not going to lose track of the labor market, and we're going to continue to be careful in our deliberations so that we can really dissect whether those shocks are going to roll off or whether they're going to compound, and whether we think that underlying inflation is gaining momentum or it's not." Of note: This framing differs from a view that monetary policy is out of whack with the broader state of the economy and needs adjustment, as heard from some of the more hawkish voices on the committee. Daly's argument implies openness to being done with rate hikes if geopolitical events cooperate in the coming weeks and months. By contrast, some of her colleagues see an economy with broader inflationary forces at play that compel an adjustment to the monetary dials. "In my view, given changes to the economy, we were out of position, and we made an adjustment in the right direction," Fed governor Michael Barr said last month .

f2db66eea0e9.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/saudi-arabia-says-3-injured-in-attacks-on-its-airports-as-fighting-with-houthis-reignites Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Saudi Arabia says 3 injured in attacks on its airports as fighting with Houthis reignites World Oct 6, 2026 2:25 PM EDT Saudi Arabia said three people were injured in the latest attacks on its airports since fighting with Yemen's Houthi rebels reignited. Meanwhile, Palestinian officials said Israeli airstrikes in Gaza City killed two people, while condemning home demolitions in east Jerusalem and violence in the occupied West Bank. Israelis are readying to mark the third anniversary of the Palestinian militant Hamas group's Oct. 7, 2023 attack as conflict in the Middle East has spread to include Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Tuesday. Full coverage is available here. Saudis say 2 airports were hit Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said airports in the cities of Najran and Jizan were hit on Monday, damaging both facilities and leaving three lightly injured. The statement didn't say who was responsible, but followed an announcement by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels that they fired missiles and drones at the kingdom. Houthi Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said in a statement on Tuesday they had fired toward a third airport on Tuesday. The Associated Press could not confirm whether the Houthis had hit Abha International Airport. Saudi authorities did not immediately comment. The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said Tuesday it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthis toward Khamis Mushait, a city in southwestern Saudi Arabia that's home to a major Saudi military base. Fighting in Yemen grinds on The Houthis were fighting Tuesday around Dhubab, a strategic town in Yemen that its internationally recognized government had previously said it had retaken, a senior Yemeni military official told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. READ MORE: Saudi-backed coalition forces Houthis from several areas around key strait, Yemeni officials say Saudi Arabia and its allies in Yemen's government have launched a military campaign to reclaim Houthi-controlled territory near the southern tip of the Red Sea to prevent disruptions to oil being exported out of the region. By Ahmed al Haj in Aden, Yemen. Tanker hit in Strait of Hormuz An outbound tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an "unknown projectile" on Monday, the British military said in a late report Tuesday. There were no immediate reports of casualties or environmental impact. Even as Iran has lost its near-complete chokehold on the strait, the ongoing risk of Iranian attacks keeps overall ship traffic well below prewar levels. 2 killed in Israeli strike in Gaza Two Israeli airstrikes killed two people in Gaza City, health officials at the city's Shifa Hospital said. Israel's military said it targeted militants in both strikes. It was the latest deadly attack since a ceasefire took effect nearly a year ago in the Israel-Hamas war triggered by the 2023 attack, when Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people, most civilians, in southern Israel and abducted 251 others. More than 1,460 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead. Netanyahu warns of potential attack related to Israel's upcoming vote Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at a Cabinet meeting on Tuesday that Hamas could attack Israel in a bid to influence the outcome of the country's elections later this month. Netanyahu, who is locked in a tough battle for re-election, did not publicly provide evidence for the claim. In recent days, Netanyahu's political opponents have pointed to the thwarted FlyDubai cockpit attack as the latest example of his government's failure to manage security threats. AFP photojournalist says Israeli settlers beat him in olive harvest season attack Jaafar Ishtyeh, a veteran Palestinian photojournalist for Agence France-Presse, said he was filming the olive harvest in the West Bank village of Aqraba when he heard shooting by Israeli settlers. He said they later encircled him, took his camera as he was filming the attack and beat him, causing injuries that required hospitalization. The Palestinian Authority said settlers in the area also shot one man in the leg and severely beat two others in the town south of Nablus. Israel's military did not provide immediate comment on the attack. The attack was the latest this harvest season, during which four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 injured, according to Palestinian officials. Israel demolishes Palestinian apartments in east Jerusalem Israeli authorities tore down a five-story building in east Jerusalem on Tuesday. National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir attended the demolition and said that Israeli authorities had demolished more than 10,000 structures built without permits over the past year and a half. Palestinians say the process of procuring construction permits is nearly impossible for them in east Jerusalem, which Israel annexed in the 1967 Mideast war and is home to almost 400,000 Palestinians. 1d12a0353010.text: President Trump's Justice Department moved to revoke citizenship from 40 naturalized citizens accused of crimes in recent months, representing what Attorney General Todd Blanche called the "largest denaturalization effort in modern history." The big picture: The Trump administration has made denaturalization a priority, moving personnel to pursue more cases and setting a goal of 250 cases by this month. Driving the news: The DOJ filed 40 denaturalization actions in district courts spanning coast to coast between Aug. 21 and Oct. 2, according to a Monday statement . "Every single one of these individuals lied their way into U.S. citizenship," Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said in a statement. Context: Denaturalization cases have a high burden of proof, and to revoke someone's citizenship, the DOJ must file a revocation action in federal district court. The general grounds for revocation, per U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, are illegal procurement of naturalized citizenship or lying to get it. "For civil revocation of naturalization, the burden of proof is clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence which does not leave the issue in doubt," per USCIS. Zoom in: Individuals named in Monday's statement had been convicted of or pleaded guilty to an array of offenses, including conspiracy to commit money laundering, sexual abuse of a minor and aggravated sodomy. What we're watching: The DOJ did not immediately respond to Axios' request for specifics on how many actions had been filed since the start of the second Trump administration. In April, the New York Times reported that the DOJ had identified 384 foreign-born Americans whose citizenship the department wanted to revoke. The following month, Axios' Brittany Gibson reported that USCIS lawyers had been temporarily moved to U.S. attorneys' offices to work on denaturalization cases. Discovery on Tuesday, ushering in a new Hollywood giant. The merger brings two of America's oldest moviemaking studios together under a new name: Skydance. The deal, which followed a tumultuous, roughly yearlong fight, further concentrates power in an industry already run by just a handful of major players. WATCH: What the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger settlement means for Hollywood HBO Max, titles ranging from "Harry Potter" to "Sinners" and networks such as CNN now find themselves under the same roof as Paramount+, CBS and the likes of "Top Gun" and "The Godfather." "Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," Ellison said in a statement Tuesday. "We couldn't be more excited to get to work." Including billions of dollars in debt, the Warner acquisition amounts to nearly $111 billion. WATCH: The politics behind the $8B Paramount-Skydance merger Ellison's Skydance bought Paramount for $8 billion last year before setting its sights on Warner. What followed was one of the biggest tie-ups ever in the media and entertainment industry. Netflix gets into a bidding war with Paramount for Warner The early days of Paramount's quest for Warner turned into a messy bidding war. Months after disclosing it was open to selling parts or even all of its business, Warner initially struck a studio and streaming deal with Netflix in December. But Skydance-owned Paramount, which claimed Warner management "never engaged meaningfully" with its previous proposals, soon launched a hostile counterbid aimed at taking over the entire company — including CNN and Discovery. WATCH: What Netflix's deal to buy Warner Bros. means for one of Hollywood's oldest studios The Hollywood giants spent much of early 2026 in a heated back-and-forth over who had a stronger offer, with Warner leadership repeatedly backing Netflix as its preferred suitor. But Paramount eventually upped its offer to buy all of Warner for $31 per share, and Netflix bowed out of the race. Warner and Paramount inked a mutual merger agreement by late February. Hollywood stars made their thoughts known Hollywood was closely watching the fight over Warner's future. From awards shows to online petitions, A-list celebrities and other creatives made their voices known. In April, thousands of movie stars, writers, directors and other professionals announced their "unequivocal opposition" to the Paramount-Warner merger. An open letter — which was signed by long-outspoken critics of the deal like Jane Fonda and Mark Ruffalo, as well as Hollywood heavyweights from Denis Villeneuve to J.J. Abrams — warned of fewer jobs and "less choice for audiences in the United States and around the world." WATCH: Paramount's Warner Bros. bid and threat to leave California divide Hollywood Others lined up to back Paramount as Ellison reiterated his commitments to the movies. At CinemaCon, the company debuted a glossy mini movie about the studio directed by Jon M. Chu and narrated by Tom Cruise — who ended the spot atop the iconic Paramount water tower, with the words "the future is paramount and the future looks pretty great from here." Director James Cameron also doubled down on his support of Ellison. The prospect of a new Warner owner also loomed over awards season, from #BlockTheMerger pins to more subtle nods in acceptance speeches. When accepting her Emmy last month, "Remarkably Bright Creatures" actor Sally Field — who also signed the open letter in opposition to the Paramount-Warner deal — stressed that "unique storytelling matters" and "we can't let those voices be silenced, or compromised or merged." WATCH: Proposed Warner Bros. sale prompts concerns among Hollywood's creative community Many industry critics were also outspoken when Netflix's studio and streaming deal was on the table, with a particular focus on the future of movies staying in theaters. Trump has attacked CNN President Donald Trump has regularly attacked reporting he deems unfavorable at CNN (most recently attempting to bar the outlet from the White House altogether). Over the course of the Warner buyout, his administration wasn't afraid to chime in about hopes for a new owner. READ MORE: CNN says it was left off Air Force One for Trump's Saturday trip to a college football game Days after Paramount launched its hostile bid for Warner last year, Trump said that CNN spread "poison and lies," adding that "I think the people who have run CNN for the last long period of time are a disgrace" and "it's imperative that CNN be sold." The White House took aim again at CNN in March, over the network's coverage of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told reporters that "the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better." Ellison has said editorial independence will be maintained at CNN. Skydance is retaining Mark Thompson as CNN's editor-in-chief. Under a settlement finalized last month with states that had sued over the takeover, the company agreed to form a "News Editorial Independence Board." c73c7453d94e.text: By — Nicolas Garriga, Associated Press Nicolas Garriga, Associated Press By — Oleg Cetinic, Associated Press Oleg Cetinic, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/french-police-fire-tear-gas-as-more-than-250000-protest-nationwide-for-school-funding Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter French police fire tear gas as more than 250,000 protest nationwide for school funding World Oct 6, 2026 2:05 PM EDT PARIS (AP) — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support school pupils demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron. As pupils again blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron's nearly decade-long tenure. "We need to listen to them," said Léa Monimart, a demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. "They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It's important to show that there are adults who support them." The Interior Ministry estimated that 256,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square during a largely peaceful march through the city. The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in "almost all cases" and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students' concerns and find solutions. Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced "ultra violence" threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any "accidents" would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a "lie." Class boycotts with police making thousands of arrests More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,100 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign. Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make "any sense to hit minors." "Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas," said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests. The violence is "absolutely unbearable," Le Coq said. Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers' riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured. READ MORE: Student protests grip France as Prime Minister Lecornu calls crisis meeting The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can't run for a third consecutive term. Against that backdrop, pupils' complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience. "You say 'young people are the future,' so listen to them," read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school. Ministry offers online portal for complaints At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris' 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade. Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry. Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see. Student protests have drawn attention to rundown classrooms At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch. "They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children's rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands," said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents. Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France's national motto: "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity." Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students' compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.
